summary: New research by The National Conversation has ranked London's 32 boroughs based on a sense of community, loneliness, neighbour trust, and civic participation. Richmond-upon-Thames ranked highest in London with a score of 91 out of 100, while Barking and Dagenham ranked last in England with a score of 8. To gather a more complete picture, researchers have launched a public survey managed by the Independent Commission on Community and Cohesion.
key_points: The National Conversation analyzed official government data to score local authorities across England on community connection.
Richmond-upon-Thames scored the highest in London at 91/100, with low loneliness and high neighborhood belonging.
Barking and Dagenham scored the lowest in England at 8/100, reflecting low trust and poor neighborhood connection.
A public survey has been launched by the Independent Commission on Community and Cohesion to gather residents' personal views on their local areas.

title: Not 'poor enough': Do people use London's pay-it-forward schemes?
author: Rosa Rahimi
content:
![People standing outside a shop with green awning and the lettering 'Lala Books'](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/d520/live/0a33aea0-9d5b-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Lala Books operates a pay-it-forward scheme funded by donations from the community
- Published
Maybe you've come across a sign like this before. It reads: "If you need a little something, but circumstances are challenging for whatever reason, take a heart and hand it to us at the counter, no explanation needed."
These are known as pay-it-forward schemes. It's when people can donate into a pot of money that can be claimed by others to cover the cost of things like a coffee or a book.
Amid the rising cost of living, schemes like these have the potential to offset the burden of small costs that can feel increasingly expensive. But how often do they get used? And do people feel comfortable using them?
![The interior of a church and people sitting, using it as a cafe space](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/d5c0/live/abd42a40-9d57-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Host Cafe runs a "suspended coffee" scheme
Host Cafe, in the heart of the City of London, is home to one of these schemes.
Based in the St Mary Aldermary church, cafe manager Barbara Gornicka says there aren't many set rules: it can be used by anyone who feels like they need the cost of their drink covered that day.
Instead of coming up to the counter and asking for a free beverage, people are also welcome to take one of the polymer clay hearts on the drinks board.
"This is to keep people from maybe being embarrassed, especially if there's a larger queue. Not everyone can just outright say: 'Can I have a free drink?'" explained Gornicka.
![A black chalkboard sign with three hearts hanging off it and a list of drinks and their prices. The top of the sign reads: Suspended Coffee, a little act of kindness by one... to another.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/fe33/live/dd94ad20-9d57-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Customers can take a polymer clay heart up to the counter to claim their free drink, no explanation needed
One regular is Paul Atherton, who was awarded the Freedom of the City of London earlier this year and has been dealing with homelessness for 17 years.
"I wouldn't have survived in this city if I didn't have the ability to sit, use Wi-Fi, and grab a coffee and feel like a part of society," he said.
Atherton, who is a filmmaker, author, and social campaigner, called schemes like this "life-changing".
After accounting for Â£160 a month in storage costs, Atherton says he lives on Â£4 a day.
![A man sits in a church cafe wearing a red shirt and a black hat with sunglasses on top.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/2f8a/live/216c8900-9d58-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Paul Atherton called schemes like these "life-changing"
"If these things didn't exist, you'd be outside of society. A cup of coffee on my current benefits is more than what I get on my daily allowance."
Prof Joan Costa-i-Font, an economist at the London School of Economics calls schemes like this a "drop in the ocean".
"It's better than no coffee," he said. "But it's not really solving the structural problem. It's a sign of kindness. I would say all these are signals of kindness."
It can also be difficult to advertise the scheme, says Gornicka, who wants it to be used more often and by people from different backgrounds.
"My goal eventually for the scheme is not to only exist for people who absolutely cannot afford a coffee, but for people to feel secure in that they can use it â even if they definitely could afford a beverage."
'I feel bad âÂ a lot of people say that'
There is a similar sentiment south of the river at Lala Books, an independent bookshop in Camberwell operating a similar scheme.
Owner Danielle Moylan says their fund can be used by anyone to claim fully or partially the cost of a book or a magazine at her store.
The scheme is especially popular with young people in the community, who are feeling the squeeze with rising rents and the cost of living â though using it can come with hesitation.
![The interior of a book store with a display of magazines to the right, a coffee machine in the centre, and a black chalkboard sign that reads: Pay It Forward, Â£2701.77 donated so far by our wonderful community. Use this to cover your book if you're short.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/c2bb/live/43e29910-9d59-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
The scheme at Lala Books is funded by the community and allows customers to claim all or part of the cost of a book
"'I feel bad' â a lot of people say that, or you can tell they don't think it's for them. Or they might not be in quotes poor enough to use it or disadvantaged enough."
But Moylan says that's not the purpose of the scheme, which exists for anyone who might feel like they don't have quite enough money to pay for a new book.
"It's just there for you to feel comfortable enough to take a book home with you," she explained.
While people can simply come up to the till and ask to use the funds, they've also come up with a more discreet method.
At a box in the back of the shop, there is a stack of envelopes filled with gift vouchers that can be picked up by anyone.
Moylan says they look exactly like their regular gift vouchers: "We wouldn't know the difference."
![A sign with the name LALA and an image of a crocodile. Text below reads: Pay it forward, forward, forward with arrows between the words and a smiley face. The sign also says: Unable to afford a book right now? These gift vouchers for Â£5, Â£10, and Â£15, kindly paid for by our wonderful community are available to help make reading accessible for everyone. No strings attached and no questions asked. Please take one if you need it. If you'd like to contribute to our pay it forward scheme, please speak to a staff member. Happy reading!](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/8226/live/7ecfbdf0-9d59-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
A sign in the back of the shop guides people to a box of gift vouchers
![A box with envelopes standing upright containing gift vouchers](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/7093/live/869b9770-9d59-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
The vouchers look exactly like any other gift voucher
Do they worry if this no-questions-asked approach could lead to people taking advantage of the scheme?
Moylan responds with a resounding no. "That's sometimes the pointy end of running a scheme like this, and that's just something you have to accept as part of a community fund."
She has had one customer tell her they used the scheme to buy a book for their friend's birthday. In another instance, the scheme was used to supply 30 books for a local primary school.
"There's something nice about the idea that people in Camberwell and Southwark are giving money â that then is going to buy books for kids who live around the corner," said Gillian Lewis, the parent who saw Lala's scheme and thought of the school books idea.
Moylan added: "We even get people who might use it one week when they feel like they don't have just quite enough money to get the book that they want, and then like two months later they'll come back and say they want to donate into it now."
Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
summary: Pay-it-forward schemes in London, such as those at Host Cafe and Lala Books, allow community donations to cover the costs of items like coffee and books for those in need. While these initiatives provide a helpful cushion amid the rising cost of living, organizers note that users often experience hesitation or feel they are not "poor enough" to use them. To reduce embarrassment, businesses use discreet methods like polymer clay hearts or identical gift vouchers, though experts view the schemes as small acts of kindness rather than structural fixes.
key_points: Host Cafe operates a suspended coffee scheme where customers can use polymer clay hearts to discreetly claim a free drink without asking directly.
Lala Books in Camberwell runs a community-funded book scheme and uses a box of indistinguishable gift vouchers to help customers take home books without feeling judged.
Organizers emphasize that the schemes are meant for anyone who feels they do not have quite enough money, rather than strictly being reserved for the severely impoverished.
Economist Prof Joan Costa-i-Font describes the schemes as a "drop in the ocean" that signals kindness but does not solve structural financial problems.
Some participants note that users may cycle between using the scheme when short on cash and later donating back into it when their circumstances improve.

title: Reduced SWR rail service continues due to dry weather
author: Richard Green
content:
![A South Western Railway train alongside the tracks on a sunny day.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1056/cpsprodpb/6320/live/5c59e4e0-9afb-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
SWR said the reduced timetable would stay in place until there was "significant rainfall"
- Published
A rail operator has confirmed its reduced timetable will remain in place because of the dry weather.
South Western Railway (SWR) and Network Rail Wessex said the service between Exeter St Davids and London Waterloo would remain two-hourly and speed restrictions would continue until there was "significant rainfall".
The Salisbury to Exeter Rail User Group (SERUG) has described the early morning timetable as "unacceptable" for commuters in east Devon.
Last year, the reduced timetable stayed in place until November 29 but SWR and NR Wessex's managing director Lawrence Bowman said the timetable would be restored "as soon as possible".
![Nick Hurrell has thin, short, grey hair and he is wearing a red and white checked shirt as he stands in front a railway train station.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/3610/live/fbe90880-9afe-11f1-b792-a710e56a11dc.jpg)
Nick Hurrell said the reduced timetable was "unacceptable"
SERUG secretary Nick Hurrell said while the new timetable showed improvements on last years' revisions, it was not serving passengers.
He said: "The worst thing about this end of the line [between Yeovil Junction and Exeter St Davids] is that it's a two-hourly service even in the morning when people and school children want to commute.
"There's over one million people per year who use the line between Axminster, Honiton and Exeter and most of those are travelling west rather than east and to have a two-hourly service simply isn't acceptable."
![Lawrence Bowman has short light brown hair and is wearing a blue blazer and white shirt. He is standing in front of a South Western Railway liveried train.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/7b59/live/597eb490-9aff-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Lawrence Bowman said engineers had removed hundreds of trees at 17 sites along the route
Bowman said "soil moisture deficit" had occurred due to the hot weather but he did understand passengers' frustration and recognised "how important the railway is to the people of the South West".
He said engineers had removed hundreds of trees at 17 sites along the track and had laid 5,000 tonnes of ballast to help maintain the track integrity.
Bowman said: "We are going to be working day and night to try and get the stability of the tracks back.
"We haven't yet seen if significant rainfall will come through September and the autumn, but rest assured, we'll be doing everything possible to get the full service back as soon as we possibly can".
Follow BBC Devon on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to spotlight@bbc.co.uk, external.
summary: South Western Railway and Network Rail Wessex have confirmed that a reduced two-hourly timetable and speed restrictions between Exeter St Davids and London Waterloo will remain in place due to dry weather and soil moisture deficit. Rail officials stated the measures will continue until there is significant rainfall, although they plan to restore the full service as soon as possible. Passenger groups have criticized the schedule, particularly the limited morning service for commuters and school children in east Devon.
key_points: A reduced two-hourly timetable and speed restrictions remain in place between Exeter St Davids and London Waterloo due to dry weather.
The restrictions will continue until the region experiences significant rainfall.
The Salisbury to Exeter Rail User Group criticized the early morning timetable as unacceptable for commuters.
Engineers have removed hundreds of trees and laid 5,000 tonnes of ballast to maintain track integrity.
Rail officials intend to restore the full service as soon as possible.

title: Filming to take place outside Houses of Parliament for Netflix drama
author: George Lithgow
content:
Members of the public could spot actors playing armed police alongside simulated emergency responses around the Houses of Parliament this coming weekend.
Production business Bad Wolf, behind television series including Doctor Who, His Dark Materials and Industry, will film scenes across the parliamentary estate and on the River Thames on 22 and 23 August.
Specialist vehicles will also feature in the area during production, with clear warning signs displayed to inform the public that filming is taking place.
Bad Wolf is reportedly working on a Netflix adaptation called The Lords’ Day, centred on a siege inside the famous building. Adapted from the novel by Michael Dobbs, the drama is set during the State Opening of Parliament.
The cast includes Damon Idris, Harry Lawtey, Arsema Thomas, Sophie Willan, Gemma Whelan and Timothy Spall.
A plot synopsis reads: “On the State Opening of Parliament, British spy Harry Jones (Damson Idris) finds himself inside the Palace of Westminster amid a lockdown.
“As a hostage siege escalates, loyalties are tested and selfless sacrifices are made, leading to a desperate fight for survival where not everyone will emerge alive.
“Can Harry use his skills and training to be the country’s savior? Adapted from a novel by Michael Dobbs (House of Cards), this is a fast-paced action thriller set in the heart of British power.”
A UK Parliament spokesperson said: “A licensed film production is taking place on and around parts of the parliamentary estate over the weekend.
“Members of the public may see actors portraying armed police officers, specialist vehicles and simulated incidents as part of the filming.
“These activities are part of a controlled and authorised production, and there is no incident or emergency on the parliamentary estate.”
Filming has previously taken place inside the Houses of Parliament for productions including Darkest Hour, Suffragette and Anatomy Of A Scandal.
summary: Production company Bad Wolf will film scenes for the Netflix drama The Lords' Day outside the Houses of Parliament and on the River Thames on August 22 and 23. The production will feature actors playing armed police, specialist vehicles, and simulated emergency responses with warning signs for the public. Adapted from Michael Dobbs' novel, the action thriller centers on a hostage siege during the State Opening of Parliament.
key_points: Filming for the Netflix drama The Lords' Day will take place around the Houses of Parliament on August 22 and 23.
The production involves actors portraying armed police, specialist vehicles, and simulated emergency incidents.
The drama is adapted from a novel by Michael Dobbs and stars Damson Idris as a British spy trapped in a hostage siege.
Parliamentary officials confirmed the filming is fully controlled and authorized, posing no actual emergency.

title: Convicted killer in UK illegally jailed for murdering London flatmate in row over £5
author: Matt Watts
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Arrest footage of Eugeniu Neamtu, 59, for the murder of his 63-year-old flatmate Gheorghe Trica](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/18/17/29/Neamtu.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
Neamtu had stabbed Mr Trica in the heart in”strikingly similar” circumstances to an earlier killing in his home country dating back to 2006, the court heard.
Read More
In May 2007, he was jailed for 15 years in Romania for murdering his housemate by stabbing him repeatedly in the chest in a drunken row over money.
He failed to declare his previous conviction or his intention to work to UK authorities and was therefore not in the country lawfully at the time of the killing in 2026, the court heard.
Neamtu had shown “no remorse” and his previous conviction in Romania was an “extremely aggravating factor”, he said.
![Gheorghe Trica](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/18/17/35/Gheorghe-Trica.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Judge Marks told Neamtu: “The fact you killed another person within three years of your release underlines how dangerous an individual you are.”
The facts of the two killings were “remarkably similar”, with both involving the use of a knife in a domestic setting in a row over money, he said.
During the trial, prosecutor Philip Evans KC told jurors there had been an argument between the defendant and Mr Trica at the flat they shared with six other Romanians in Walthamstow.
Both had shouted insults in Romanian and Mr Trica was heard to say: “Give me back those £5.”
At one point a bystander exclaimed “Oh my God, he has cut Trica” and the victim was found in a pool of blood, jurors were told.
Mr Trica collapsed on the communal balcony outside the front door of the flat and died at the scene, despite efforts of police and medics.
Afterwards, the defendant was seen to throw something over the banister of the balcony.
A police dog was used to search the area and the murder weapon – a black-handled steak knife – was recovered from the garden.
In a call translated by a Romanian-speaking interpreter, Neamtu told a 999 operator: “There was an incident here and a person is injured. There was an altercation, a man was cut, and I am the perpetrator.”
Following his arrest, Neamtu claimed in prepared statements that Mr Trica had threatened to kill him, pushed him down the stairs and made throat-slitting gestures.
He said he picked up the knife from the kitchen to “scare” Mr Trica and stabbed him in the chest to protect himself.
![Eugeniu Neamtu, 59, fatally stabbed a flatmate in the chest (METROPOLITAN POLICE/PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/21/11/a8b597d17fcb57bae81d3b3d66d7a866Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3MzkwNTAx-2.85603482.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Mr Evans pointed out “striking similarities” to an earlier stabbing in Romania for which Neamtu was found guilty and jailed in May 2007.
In August 2006, Neamtu had repeatedly stabbed Adrian Vas in the chest at the house where they were both living.
The pair had been drinking plum brandy and rowed over rent and work that the defendant had agreed to carry out at the property.
During the confrontation, the defendant took up a knife from the hallway and attacked Mr Vas, jurors were told.
That knife was later recovered from the grounds of the property.
The defendant told Romanian authorities that he and Mr Vas had argued, insulted each other and fought with objects to hand, and that it was possible he struck Mr Vas with a knife in self‑defence.
In later accounts, he said that he picked up a knife because he was afraid and that Mr Vas had provoked him, the court was told.
The Romanian court rejected the defendant’s claim of self‑defence.
Mr Evans had told jurors: “The prosecution in this case relies on this previous conviction because of the striking similarities between the circumstances of that offence and the allegation you are concerned with in this trial.
“In both cases the defendant was involved in a drunken argument with an associate over money. In both cases he took up a knife from within the home.
“In both cases he stabbed the other man in the chest. In both cases he later claimed that he acted in self‑defence.”
Neamtu, of Westbury Road, Walthamstow, was assisted by an interpreter in court. He denied murder but declined to give evidence in his trial.
The jury deliberated for three hours to find him guilty of murder.
The jury was not told that Neamtu’s first victim had in fact died until after reaching its verdict.
A Home Office spokesperson said: “Our thoughts are with the victim of this horrific crime and with all those who have been affected by it.
“The perpetrator has now been rightly convicted and justice has been delivered by the courts. Once sentencing has taken place, we will seek to deport him off British soil.”
summary: Eugeniu Neamtu was convicted of murdering his 63-year-old flatmate, Gheorghe Trica, by stabbing him in the chest during a drunken argument over £5 in a Walthamstow flat. It was revealed during the proceedings that Neamtu was living in the UK illegally and had previously been jailed for 15 years in Romania in 2007 for a strikingly similar murder of another housemate over money. Judge Marks highlighted Neamtu's dangerousness, and the Home Office stated an intention to deport him following sentencing.
key_points: Eugeniu Neamtu stabbed his flatmate Gheorghe Trica in the heart during a dispute over £5 in Walthamstow.
Neamtu was in the UK unlawfully, having failed to declare a previous 2007 murder conviction in Romania.
The 2007 Romanian conviction involved remarkably similar circumstances, where Neamtu stabbed a housemate in the chest during a money dispute and claimed self-defence.
A jury found Neamtu guilty of murder after three hours of deliberation.
The Home Office announced plans to deport Neamtu following his sentencing.

title: More than meets the 'London Eye': Over two thirds of tourists leave capital with an unfinished bucket list - London TV
author: London-TV
content:
New research has revealed that more than two-thirds (69%) of international tourists leave London with sights still left to see, while the majority say the capital is even more impressive in person than it appears online.
The research, commissioned by The Original Tour, suggests that no amount of scrolling, planning or viral travel recommendations can prepare visitors for just how much there is to discover in London.
While Googling destinations or scrolling for inspiration helps shape visitors’ expectations before they arrive, the research shows that the real-life experience surpasses what most tourists see on screen. Over half (58%) of French visitors and two-thirds (67%) of Spanish visitors say London is significantly more impressive in person than it appears across social media, films and television.
With so much left to discover, tourists are not only keen to return to London themselves, but are also clear on which sights they think first-time visitors should prioritise:
The Desire to Return: More than three-quarters (79%) of tourists say they are likely to return specifically to explore the sights they ran out of time to see, and 85% are likely to visit London again within the next five years.
The Must-See Landmarks: Buckingham Palace tops the list of landmarks tourists would recommend to first-time visitors, with 35% naming it a must-see, followed by Big Ben and the Houses of Parliament (31%) and The London Eye (29%).
While international tourists gravitate toward classic landmark architecture, domestic and demographic data reveal distinct priorities across age groups and UK regions. Older visitors aged 65 and over strongly champion historic heritage, with over half (50%) recommending the Tower of London alongside free museums and galleries (37%).
In contrast, younger travellers focus on lifestyle experiences. 18-to-24-year-olds are three times more likely to recommend London food and dining (23%) than over-65s (8%), while 25-to-34-year-olds favour The London Eye (36%).
Regionally, visitors from the North East lead recommendations for London’s markets like Borough and Camden (42%), South West tourists also heavily favour free museums and galleries (40%), and Scottish visitors are among the most eager to recommend a West End show (32%).
Other findings from the research include:
Social Dining: Three in five (60%) travellers used social media specifically to choose where to eat or drink during their trip, highlighting the continued influence of online recommendations on visitors’ decisions.
Planned Experiences: The majority (59%) of travellers said their favourite experience in London was one they had carefully planned and sought out themselves, highlighting how visitors are taking an increasingly considered approach to making the most of their time in the capital.
For visitors keen to make the most of their time in London and avoid missing out on its must-see sights, sightseeing bus tours offer one of the most convenient and effective ways to take in the capital’s best attractions in one journey. With carefully designed routes and expertly curated commentary available in 10 languages, visitors can see the landmarks they may have already spotted online, while discovering the stories, history and culture behind them.
image.png
Credit: The Original Tour
As the creators of the Hop-on Hop-off sightseeing bus tour, The Original Tour has spent 75 years helping visitors discover London. As the only sightseeing operator solely focused on the capital, it has built specialist knowledge of the city, creating carefully curated tours that bring together its most iconic sights, hidden gems and stories. With a complimentary Thames River Cruise included, visitors can see even more of London’s most recognisable sights in one experience, making it a convenient way to make the most of their time in the capital, however long or short their stay. From royal landmarks such as Buckingham Palace to riverside views and cultural hotspots, its experienced guides bring London’s history and culture to life, offering visitors a chance to see a different side of the capital while taking in many of its most recognisable sights.
The research highlights the enduring appeal of experiencing London in person, while showing that social media and digital travel content continue to influence how visitors plan their trips. With carefully curated itineraries often leaving visitors struggling to fit everything in, the findings suggest there is still no substitute for experiencing the capital for yourself. Terry Gabriel, Chief Manager at The Original Tour, commented on this, saying:
“We are seeing a clear shift in how visitors approach London. Travellers may arrive with certain expectations shaped by short online clips and carefully curated itineraries, but once they experience the capital for themselves, they discover that its true scale, energy and atmosphere simply cannot be captured on a screen.
“With almost 7 out of 10 visitors saying they ran out of time, and many planning to return specifically to explore what they missed, it is clear that there is always more to discover in London. More than can fit in one Instagram Reel or TikTok. As we celebrate 75 years of sightseeing, we want to show visitors why London is one of the world’s most impressive cities, sharing the stories and local knowledge that bring the city’s most iconic landmarks to life.”
No two tours are ever quite the same. The different seasons, changing events across the city and diverse mix of passengers on board all help create a unique experience each time. Whether visitors are seeing London for the first time or rediscovering familiar landmarks, a sightseeing tour offers a fresh perspective on London. Because in a city with so much to see, you’re never truly LON-DONE!?
The research is a reminder that no itinerary, social media post or digital guide can capture everything a city like London has to offer. For those visiting, there will always be another landmark to discover, another story to hear and another reason to return
summary: New research commissioned by The Original Tour reveals that over two-thirds of international tourists leave London with unfinished bucket lists because the capital surpasses its online portrayal. The study shows that 79% of visitors are likely to return specifically to see sights they missed, with Buckingham Palace topping the list of recommended landmarks. Furthermore, preferences vary by age and region, with older visitors favoring historic sites and younger travelers prioritizing food and lifestyle experiences.
key_points: Over two-thirds (69%) of international tourists leave London with sights still left to see.
More than three-quarters (79%) of tourists plan to return to London to explore missed sights.
Buckingham Palace is the top recommended landmark for first-time visitors at 35%.
Younger travelers aged 18-to-24 are three times more likely to recommend London food and dining than those over 65.

title: Investigation launched after death of man in cell in London custody suite
author: Megan Howe
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/21/17/58/Croydon_Custody_Centre.jpeg?trim=226,0,278,0&quality=75&auto=webp&width=1000)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
The man had been arrested in Croydon on Wednesday afternoon after he failed to appear at Croydon Magistrates’ Court on charges of being drunk and disorderly, which led to the court issuing a no-bail warrant for his arrest, the force said.
Officers were carrying out cell checks at Windmill Road custody suite in Croydon at 12.30am on Friday when they found the man unresponsive after he became unwell.
Despite the best efforts of paramedics, the man was pronounced dead at 1.17am.
He had previously been seen by a healthcare professional and also received welfare and observation checks while in custody, the Met said.
Deputy Assistant Commissioner James Harman said: “Our thoughts are with the man’s family and loved ones following his tragic death.
“The full circumstances of this death in custody will now be independently examined and we are providing our fullest support to that IOPC investigation.”
summary: An independent investigation has been launched following the death of a man in a London custody suite. The man was arrested in Croydon on Wednesday after failing to appear in court and was found unresponsive during cell checks early Friday morning. Despite medical intervention by paramedics, he was pronounced dead at the scene.
key_points: A man died in a London custody suite after being found unresponsive during cell checks.
He was arrested on Wednesday on a no-bail warrant for failing to appear at Croydon Magistrates' Court.
He had been seen by a healthcare professional and received welfare checks while in custody.
The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) is independently examining the full circumstances of the death.

title: CCTV images released after teenage boy robbed on a London train
author: Megan Howe
content:

The group swiped his phone, ripping his jacket in the struggle, before leaving the train at Shortlands railway station, police said.

summary: British Transport Police have released CCTV images of teenage boys following a robbery on a London train. Authorities believe the individuals pictured may have information to assist the ongoing investigation.
key_points: A teenage boy was robbed of his phone on a London train.
The victim's jacket was ripped during the struggle with the group.
The suspects left the train at Shortlands railway station.
Police have released CCTV images seeking information from the public.

title: Why Sadiq Khan would win fourth term - even if most Londoners want him to stand down
author: Nicholas Cecil
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
The vast majority of Conservative and Reform UK voters would be expected to take the view that Sir Sadiq should stand down and let a different Labour candidate contest the mayoral election in 2028.
They do, by 81% and 93% respectively.
But so do four out of ten Labour supporters at the 2024 general election, according to the survey.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/21/11/01M08E0VP65W2YZY55X8VGASMT.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
More men than women in the capital believe it is time for Sir Sadiq to move on, by 58% to 54%.
Eight out of ten Londoners aged 65 and over think the Mayor should make do with three terms in office.
Two-thirds of the 50 to 64 age group take this view, as do 48% of Londoners aged 25 to 49, and 41% of 18 to 24-year-olds.
Overall, 56% of Londoners say Sir Sadiq should stand down and let a different Labour candidate contest the mayoral election in two years’ time.
So the evidence is clear on Sir Sadiq’s likely fate if he seeks another term in City Hall.
Or is it?
![Shadow local government secretary Sir James Cleverly (James Manning/PA credit)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/21/06/7b1f558ca54f435a583500ccfe63f7cdY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3MzUwMDg0-2.83975597.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Key to poll results is the questions asked.
The YouGov survey was a single question on this issue as part of a broader mayoral poll which had other findings which do not make good reading for Sir Sadiq.
Read More
But Labour remains the most popular party in London despite the turmoils of Sir Keir Starmer’s premiership.
And elections come down to who is a preferred candidate or party.
When the London mayoralty race is framed in this context, Labour and Sir Sadiq are significantly ahead of rivals.
Crucially, who the other parties select as their candidates could sway the mayoral race.
![Nigel Farage Hosts Reform UK Press Conference](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/01/07/10/58/Nigel-Farage-Hosts-Reform-UK-Press-Conference-wenuq4dq.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
But Conservative Leader Kemi Badenoch is searching far and wide for the person who would be her party’s strongest candidate.
The longer a politician holds office the more vulnerable they become to being voted out or deposed by their own party.
So, if Sir Sadiq did go for a fourth term a contest against former London Assembly member Sir James could be close, though, Labour would still be the frontrunner.
Alternatively, Ms Cunningham might succeed in getting in a two-way run-off against Labour under the supplementary vote system used for the London mayoral election.
But she may find it harder to win once second preference votes are counted.
Whoever wins will find that to govern is to choose.
As for voters, whatever their views on Sir Sadiq, they will also find that elections are to choose.
summary: A recent YouGov survey indicates that 56% of Londoners believe Mayor Sadiq Khan should stand down instead of seeking a fourth term in 2028. Opposition is particularly high among Conservative voters, Reform UK supporters, older age groups, and even a portion of 2024 Labour voters. Despite this desire for a change, Labour and Khan remain significantly ahead of their rivals when elections focus on preferred candidates and parties.
key_points: Overall, 56% of Londoners surveyed think Sadiq Khan should step down after three terms.
Opposition to a fourth term includes 81% of Conservatives, 93% of Reform UK voters, and 40% of 2024 Labour supporters.
Older demographics are most opposed, with 80% of those aged 65 and over believing he should step down.
Despite these poll numbers, Labour and Khan remain significantly ahead of their rivals in mayoral preference.
The outcome of the next election will heavily depend on the strength of the candidates selected by opposing parties.

title: Moment burglary gang busted by police trying to tunnel way into London jewellers
author: Matt Watts
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Moment crime gang busted by police trying to tunnel way into London jewellery shop in brazen heist](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/21/13/24/burglar-gang-compsoite.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
Laurentiu-Daniel Nitisoara, 38, and Ioan Asafeti, 39, broke into a neighbouring massage parlour before attempting to drill a hole into the jewellers.
The break-in Tooting on July 17 was the latest in a series of burglaries the tunnelling gang carried out on businesses in the capital - making holes in shops to bypass security systems as they stole £700,000 in goods.
Nitisoara was arrested immediately in a nearby alleyway. Following a search of the area, officers tracked down Asafeti, hiding on a rooftop and put him in handcuffs.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/21/12/52/Tunnel-burglar-led-away-at-Mitcham-jewellers.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
The footage shows officers then searching a massage parlour the pair had broken into and uncover their plan to tunnel through a wall into the neighbouring jewellery shop.
![Hole made by tunneling burglary gang at Mitcham jewellers](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/21/12/39/Screenshot-2026-08-21-135357.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
They also find bags of tools and equipment being used to dig the hole.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/21/13/01M0J52J6SC10TMFJQ3NQKMVHY.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/21/13/01M0J52FX23HS99NGFZRBFGS6H.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/21/12/01/Laurentiu-Daniel.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
An investigation, led by the Met's Flying Squad, linked the group to several burglaries across the capital between May and July in which the men mainly targeted jewellers.
Detectives gathered extensive CCTV footage showing members of the group obtaining tools and other equipment used in the offences.
Further enquiries through Interpol revealed the group had possible links to similar offences in Europe.
Read More
They will be sentenced on Friday, 23 October.
Detective Superintendent Dan Mitchell, of the Met’s Flying Squad, said: “These criminals dug their own hole after emergency response officers caught them red-handed.
“Their arrests didn't just stop this burglary. They formed part of a wider Flying Squad investigation that uncovered an organised crime group linked to a string of jewellery shop break-ins across London worth more than £700,000.
“We're driving down commercial burglary across the capital, with offences falling by 12 per cent in the past year.
“Our message to these criminals is clear: target London businesses and we'll hunt you down and put you before the courts.”
summary: Police in London busted a burglary gang attempting to tunnel through a massage parlour into a neighboring jewellery shop in Tooting. Laurentiu-Daniel Nitisoara and Ioan Asafeti were caught red-handed and arrested at the scene on July 17. The Met's Flying Squad linked the pair to a series of London burglaries targeting jewellers, resulting in £700,000 worth of stolen goods.
key_points: Laurentiu-Daniel Nitisoara and Ioan Asafeti were arrested during a break-in attempt in Tooting on July 17.
The suspects broke into a massage parlour and attempted to drill a hole through the wall into a jewellery shop.
Police and the Met's Flying Squad linked the organized crime group to multiple London jewellery burglaries totaling £700,000.
Nitisoara was arrested in an alleyway, while Asafeti was found hiding on a rooftop.
The defendants are scheduled to be sentenced on Friday, October 23.

title: A new immersive exhibition and archive will celebrate Romford’s underrated electronic music history
author: Eloise Feilden
content:
[title]
As topics for an art exhibition go, an immersive exploration of Romford’s ’90s music scene might seem pretty niche. But the east London ’burb was an influential hub for the Big Smoke’s sound at the time. Record shop Boogie Times, labels including Suburban Base, pirate radio stations, promoters and producers all called Romford home during that decade, and helped shape a scene which made waves well beyond the RM postcode.
When it opens in October, Mega Mega: Romford’s Suburban Sound Revolution will explore just how big an influence the area had on electronic music and club culture in the capital, from hardcore and jungle to garage and drum and bass.
Running from October until December, it’ll be a deep dive combining audio elements with archive material and first-hand stories from people who lived through the era. Havering borough is even calling on locals to get involved ahead of the opening to share their personal tales and donate to the archive.
![Mega Mega: Romford’s Suburban Sound Revolution](https://media.timeout.com/images/106438971/image.webp) 
Once the exhibition comes to a close, the local authority will gather everything into a publicly accessible archive so you can dig into its musical history whenever you fancy.
Romford's wider cultural footprint shouldn't be overlooked. The town is also home to Lumiere Romford, a community-led cinema which has gained a cult following as the only picture house in the UK which pays its members. Cool, huh?
Did you see that the Natural History Museum is opening a room that has been closed to the public since World War II?

Running from October to December, the event will combine audio, archive materials, and personal stories to highlight genres like jungle, hardcore, and drum and bass. After the exhibition closes, the collected materials will be preserved in a publicly accessible local authority archive.
key_points: Romford was a major hub for 1990s electronic music, including pirate radio, record labels, and producers.
The exhibition runs from October to December and features audio elements, archive materials, and first-hand accounts.

title: These fairytale spots in London feel straight out of a Disney film: From a hidden Covent Garden courtyard to a ‘little Gothic castle’, here’s where to explore this weekend
author: Charlie Maudsley
content:
![Hampstead Pergola in Hamstead Heath and Neal's Yard in Covent Garden in London](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/21131425/Photo-Collage-10-1024x683.jpg) 
London is often more hustle and bustle than ‘happily ever after’, but there are still a few corners of the city that feel straight out of a Disney film. From hidden Covent Garden courtyards with Coco-style colour to romantic Hampstead Heath terraces with Tangled vibes, these storybook spots are practically made for sunny summer wandering. There are secret gardens, Gothic towers, pretty little lanes and enough storybook architecture to make your usual weekend plans in London feel a bit more enchanting.
And if you really want to commit to the theme, you can finish the day at a candlelit Disney tribute concert taking place inside an 800-year-old cathedral (No carriage home included — the Tube will do).
Strawberry Hill, Twickenham
Strawberry Hill in Twickenham is a brilliant-white Gothic Revival villa that’s over 270 years old. Driven by a desire to create his own “little Gothic castle”, writer Horace Walpole bought a modest house on the site in 1749 and gradually transformed it into the fairytale-like villa seen today, completing the project in 1776.
The Disney flair comes from its white turrets, battlements, pointed arches and dramatic Gothic interiors — the kind of place Belle might explore in the Beast’s castle, or Aurora might wander through before pricking her finger on a spinning wheel.
📍Address: 268 Waldegrave Road, Twickenham, TW1 4ST, United Kingdom
Pergola & Hill Garden, Hamstead Heath
![an orange-hued view down a walkway in hampstead pergola](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/17170113/shutterstock_725992489-1-1024x680.jpg)
The Hampstead Pergola at Hamstead Heath was created as part of the private gardens of “The Hill,” the estate bought by William Hesketh Lever—later Lord Leverhulme—in 1904. Later additions were made over time, and by 1925, the gardens evolved into a grand Edwardian garden.
Today, you’ll find a long colonnaded pergola of Portland-stone Doric columns adorned in vines and roses. The overgrown, secret-garden vibe brings Sleeping Beauty to mind, while the lush greenery has the feel of Rapunzel’s hidden tower deep in the woods.
📍Address: Inverforth Cl, London NW3 7EX, United Kingdom
Neal’s Yard, Covent Garden
![looking up at some of the colourful buildings of neal's yard, with orange and blue windowsills and yellow frontages](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/25122501/shutterstock_128021372-1-1024x678.jpg)
Tucked away in Seven Dials, Covent Garden, Neal’s Yard is a brightly coloured courtyard that’s still easy to miss. This place adds a big splash of colour to London’s usual industrial vibe—a vibrant oasis complete with independent shops and a feel-good, slightly chaotic charm.
Its saturated colours, plants spilling from windows and close-set courtyard buildings feel like a mini London take on the Madrigal family’s vibrant village in Encanto.
📍Address: Neal’s Yard, Seven Dials, Covent Garden, London WC2H 9DP
Kyoto Garden, Holland Park
![The lovely Kyoto Garden in Holland Park – a great spot for a first date in London](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/02/11035523/romantic-places-london-kyoto-garden-1024x683.jpg)
Tucked inside Holland Park, Kyoto Garden is a peaceful little escape with a mini waterfall, koi pond, stone lanterns and Japanese maples. Donated by Kyoto’s Chamber of Commerce in 1991 and created for the Japan Festival in London, it feels like a scene from Mulan — all tranquil water, dramatic planting and storybook calm in the middle of the city. And if you’re lucky, you might spot a peacock or two wandering around the site.
📍Address: Holland Park, Holland Park Ave, London W11 4UA, United Kingdom
summary: London features several storybook locations that evoke a Disney film atmosphere for summer wandering. These enchanting spots include historic villas, grand Edwardian gardens, colorful hidden courtyards, and tranquil Japanese gardens. Visitors can also choose to conclude their explorations by attending a candlelit Disney tribute concert inside an 800-year-old cathedral.
key_points: Strawberry Hill in Twickenham is a 270-year-old Gothic Revival villa featuring white turrets and battlements.
The Hampstead Pergola at Hampstead Heath offers a grand Edwardian garden with a secret-garden vine and rose-adorned colonnade.
Neal's Yard in Covent Garden is a brightly coloured courtyard filled with independent shops and saturated hues.
Kyoto Garden in Holland Park provides a tranquil escape featuring a mini waterfall, koi pond, and wandering peacocks.

title: Legendary filmmaker Steven Soderbergh is curating a London movie season with a twist
author: Phil de Semlyen
content:
[title]
Legendary indie auteur Steven Soderbergh is coming to London for a unique run of screenings starting next month.
‘A Man Under the Influence’ will pack in nine movies over nine Thursday evenings, running from September 3 to October 30.
The Whiteley in Bayswater will host the movies – each hand-picked by the Ocean’s Eleven and Out of Sight director.
Among the films on the slate are Ernst Lubitsch’s screwball romance Trouble in Paradise, Hitchcock thriller Notorious, subversive class satire The Servant and massive-shark movie Jaws. Paul Thomas Anderson’s Fitzrovia-set Phantom Thread will bring the curtain down on this run of classics.
To add spice, each event will boost a 63-minute happy hour – it’s Soderbergh’s 63rd birthday, see – and the chance to sip on a cocktail created by a top London bar made with his favourite Bolivian spirit, Singani 63.
![A Man Under the Influence](https://media.timeout.com/images/106438529/image.webp) 
The season will be ‘a weekly film and cocktail series showcasing nine personally and culturally influential films curated by Soderbergh, one from each decade from the 1930s to 2010s and each introduced over video by the man himself. Tickets are £20.90 and the doors open at 6pm.
The full programme and cocktail partner:
- September 3 – Trouble in Paradise (1930s) 
Cocktail by Archive & Myth
- September 10 – Notorious (1940s)
Cocktail by The Mandrake
- September 17 – The 5,000 Fingers of Dr. T (1950s)
Cocktail by Cocktail Trading Company
- September 24 – The Servant (1960s)
Cocktail by Viajante 87
- October 1 – Jaws (1970s)
Cocktail by Nancy’s
- October 8 – Do the Right Thing (1980s)
Cocktail by Murder Inc.
- October 15 – Fargo (1990s)
Cocktail by The Natural Philosopher
- October 22 – Lost in Translation (2000s)
Cocktail by Equal Parts
- October 29 – Phantom Thread (2010s)
Cocktail by Hawksmoor
Soderbergh curated a similar Singani 63 season at New York’s Nitehawk Cinema at the beginning of the year.
‘The only partner we considered for the UK version of A Man Under the Influence was Everyman, whose love of movies is matched only by their commitment to the moviegoing experience,’ says Soderbergh. ‘Ask yourself: Can I resist the idea of a classic movie, Singani 63, and the groovy Everyman vibe all happening at the same time? The answer is no, you cannot, so get your butt to The Whiteley on Thursdays this fall and let's light this candle!’
London has been a home-from-home for the American director in recent times. He’s filmed his last two films, spy thriller Black Bag and art heist flick The Christophers in the city.
For tickets and more information head to the official website.
How many of 2026’s best films have you seen?
summary: Filmmaker Steven Soderbergh is curating a nine-week film and cocktail series in London titled 'A Man Under the Influence.' Running from September 3 to October 30 at The Whiteley in Bayswater, the event features hand-picked classic films from the 1930s to the 2010s. Each screening includes a 63-minute happy hour featuring custom cocktails made with Soderbergh's preferred Bolivian spirit, Singani 63.
key_points: The film series runs for nine Thursday evenings from September 3 to October 30 at The Whiteley in Bayswater.
The lineup includes movies spanning from the 1930s to the 2010s, such as Trouble in Paradise, Jaws, and Phantom Thread.
Each event features a 63-minute happy hour celebrating Soderbergh's 63rd birthday with cocktails made from Singani 63.
Tickets cost £20.90, and Soderbergh will introduce each film via video.

title: The exact date London will be hit by the sixth heatwave of the summer
author: India Lawrence
content:
[title]
Enjoying the current little cold snap? Finally, it’s been cool enough to wear a jacket and use a duvet. It’s even been raining. But don’t get too comfortable, because the UK is bracing itself for the sixth heatwave of the summer.
Londoners have sweated through five heatwaves already this season, with temperatures soaring to a sweltering 38.1C – making it the hottest summer ever recorded. Now, the Met Office’s long-range weather forecast for September, October and November has said there could be an ‘increased risk of heatwaves and heat-related impacts especially during the first half of the period’.
When will the sixth heatwave arrive in London?
According to the Met Office’s long-range forecast for August 30 to September 13, ‘there is a chance that late-season hot spells or heatwaves develop, especially in the south’. September will be filled with a mixture of showers and hot spells, followed by ‘drier, more settled weather, especially in the south and east’ for the second half of the month.
The forecast added: ‘Temperatures will probably be near normal at first, but may turn warmer later with a chance of some hot periods in the south.’
The Met Office also warned of risks of thunderstorms and flooding throughout early autumn.
![London heatwave, May 2026](https://media.timeout.com/images/106423752/image.webp) 
However, this forecast isn’t for certain and could easily change. The Met Office said that the signals for the heatwave in later September were currently ‘very weak’, meaning that it’s probably too soon to tell the exact date of the heatwave, and if it will definitely happen at all.

The Met Office's long-range forecast indicates an increased risk of late-season hot spells in the south during early autumn, alongside risks of thunderstorms and flooding. However, current signals for the heatwave are very weak, meaning the exact date and certainty of the event remain unconfirmed.

title: My London: Kelly Piquet
author: Rose Beer
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![The London Question: What's the best thing to do in the city on a sunny day?](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/19/15/34/Model-and-columnist-Kelly-Piquet.jpeg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![STYLE](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_style_embed_desktop.png)
Home is…
Monaco, where I live with my daughters, Penelope and Lily. I’ve been based there for several years and I love the balance between the sea, nature and an international lifestyle.
Where do you stay in London?
For a romantic weekend, I love the Bulgari hotel. It’s elegant, discreet and has one of my favourite spas. When I’m travelling with my daughters, I usually stay at the Connaught. The service is incredible and it is warm, comfortable and family-friendly.
Where would you recommend for a first date?
A walk around Notting Hill followed by dinner at Gold. It’s relaxed, charming and perfect for a good conversation.
![Model and columnist  Kelly Piquet](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/19/15/34/Model-and-columnist-Kelly-Piquet.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Which shops do you rely on?
Dover Street Market for fashion inspiration, Daunt for books, Space NK for skincare, Liberty for gifts and Selfridges for last-minute essentials and beauty. Their beauty floor is hard to beat and it’s where I stock up on favourites, including Anastasia Beverly Hills products.
What’s the best meal you’ve had?
Two come to mind. Dorian for its incredible food and relaxed atmosphere and Carbone London for the energy, the people-watching and the spicy rigatoni. The best meals are always about the company as much as the food.
What would you do if you were Mayor for the day?
I’d create more pedestrian-only areas, hold more outdoor fitness classes and organise a giant city-wide summer dinner party.
Who is the most iconic Londoner?
David Bowie. He was a true original who influenced music, fashion and culture.
![An exhibition of items from the David Bowie archive are to go on tour (Yui Mok/PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/07/01/00/673fcb6ca157bef0c0060604fbcab9eaY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzgyODQyNTY3-2.1972992.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Where do you go to have fun?
I love long lunches with friends, gallery visits, theatre nights and wandering around Notting Hill without a plan.
What’s the best thing a cabbie has ever said to you?
“Don’t worry love, nobody really knows where they’re going in London.”
Where do you exercise?
I usually exercise at Alo Wellness Club or by taking long walks through Hyde Park.
Have you ever had a run-in with a police officer?
Nothing exciting enough to share!
Where do you let your hair down?
Notting Hill or Mayfair with friends. We start with dinner at one of my favourite neighbourhood spots, then we’ll wander into a cosy pub or a cocktail bar with live music. I prefer places where you can actually have a conversation.
Who do you call when you want to have fun?
Close friends who always know what’s happening in the city. We keep things simple: dinner, good wine, lots of laughter and then see where the evening takes us. The company makes the night more than the venue.
What’s your biggest extravagance?
Travel. I never regret spending money on experiences. They’re the memories that stay with you. One of my favourite places is St Barths. I love its relaxed atmosphere, beautiful beaches and the way it feels understated and special at once. I also love Japan — I feel like I’m discovering something new on every visit.
What are you up to for work?
I’m balancing motherhood with content creation, brand partnerships and projects across fashion, beauty and lifestyle.
What do you collect?
Books from my travels and vintage fashion pieces. I love bringing home a book from every city I visit. As for vintage fashion, I’m always searching for timeless pieces with a story. I especially love vintage Chanel and Hermès. They’re beautifully made and I like the idea of giving something another life, rather than always buying new.
What’s your favourite work of art in London?
It’s got to be the J M W Turner paintings at Tate Britain.
When you’re in need of headspace, where do you go?
A walk through Hyde Park or along the Thames clears my mind. If I need inspiration I’ll often spend an hour wandering through a museum or gallery, especially the V&A. I always leave with new ideas and a different perspective.
As told to Rose Beer
summary: Model and columnist Kelly Piquet shares her favourite London spots, travel habits, and lifestyle preferences in a city profile. She discusses her home base in Monaco, where she stays when visiting London with her daughters, and her top recommendations for dining, shopping, and leisure. Piquet also details her work in fashion and content creation, her collections, and her go-to places for relaxation and exercise.
key_points: Kelly Piquet lives in Monaco with her daughters and stays at the Bulgari hotel or the Connaught when visiting London.
She recommends a walk in Notting Hill followed by dinner at Gold for a first date.
Her preferred London shops include Dover Street Market, Daunt, Space NK, Liberty, and Selfridges.
She balances motherhood with content creation, brand partnerships, and projects in fashion, beauty, and lifestyle.

summary: London house prices fell overall by 2.5% in the 12 months leading to June, with city centre and inner London boroughs experiencing the most significant drops of up to 25.4%. key_points: Average house prices in London fell by 2.5% in the year to June, with drops occurring in 18 boroughs and increases in 14.

title: Fare evasion could be costing TfL £211m a year- £20m than previously reported
author: Kumail Jaffer
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Higher Fines For Fare Evasion On Tube Come Into Force](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/06/19/11/19/London-fare-dodger-2.png?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
TfL say they lose £190 million annually to those who choose not to pay for their journeys on the network – a rate of around 3.5 per cent. Transport chiefs say they hope to bring the rate down to 1.5 per cent by the end of 2031.
However, they have now admitted that the amount lost could be as high as £211 million per year – far higher than the £168 million in estimated extra revenue raised from fare rises on buses and Tubes earlier this year.
The admission, made for the first time in a disclosure to the Tube Alerter website and shared with the Local Democracy Reporting Service (LDRS), is due to officials not wanting to “overstate the estimated level of revenue loss”.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/20/16/30/FA_2192.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
This means that the publicly stated figure of £190 million “represents an evidence-based assessment that takes these limitations into account.”
TfL say the adjustment is made due to staff deriving their estimates from intelligence-led activity at some locations where fare evasion is more likely to occur, and therefore “may not be fully representative of the network as a whole”.
“The estimated value of fare evasion incorporates a 10 per cent reduction to reflect the medium confidence level associated with the overall assumptions,” an internal TfL review concluded.
“This recognises the limitations of the available data and the absence of a system that automatically matches passenger journeys with payments made.”
Newer style technology, such as modern gateline infrastructure which is currently being tested in New York, will be able to more accurately track those passing through the barriers without paying, TfL predicts.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/20/16/47/FA_2189.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
The internal confidence assessment and supporting assumptions have never been published separately, officials confirmed, as they said publication of such “detailed information…could compromise TfL’s ability to prevent, detect and respond to fare evasion, ultimately impacting the protection of public revenue”.
Read More
“Instead of showing leadership and gripping the issue, he has trapped TfL in a doom loop where underestimating data leads them to not take the issue seriously, causing more underestimation.
“It is wrong, it must stop, and Londoners’ confidence must be restored that the Mayor is serious about tackling this crime that fare-paying commuters are expected to pick up the £200m bill for.”
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/20/17/17/FA_2370.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
A TfL spokesperson said: “Robust analysis of fare evasion on London’s transport network is a vital tool in tackling it, and the estimated total cost of fare evasion is just one of many figures we produce to measure the scale of the issue.
“All figures produced are estimates that are calculated according to TfL’s best interpretation of the data, in line with industry standards.
“The estimated cost of £190m represents an evidence-based assessment that takes limitations of the data used into account.”
summary: Transport for London (TfL) has admitted that fare evasion could be costing the network up to £211 million a year, which is significantly higher than the previously reported £190 million. TfL officials previously used a conservative, evidence-based assessment to avoid overstating revenue losses due to limitations in available data. Transport chiefs aim to reduce the overall fare evasion rate from about 3.5 per cent down to 1.5 per cent by the end of 2031.
key_points: Fare evasion on TfL may cost up to £211 million annually, which is £20 million higher than previously stated figures.
TfL officially reports a lower £190 million loss as an evidence-based assessment that accounts for data limitations.
Estimates incorporate a 10 per cent reduction due to medium confidence levels and the lack of a system matching journeys to payments.
TfL hopes to lower the current 3.5 per cent fare evasion rate to 1.5 per cent by the end of 2031.

title: What does 'strongest El Niño in living memory' mean for London's weather?
author: Tom Place
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![El Nino threatens food security: World food programme warns of hunger crisis](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/01/15/13/31/BRITAIN-WEATHER-RAIN-9vporjir.jpeg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
An El Niño event is declared when sea surface temperatures in the tropical eastern Pacific rise to 0.5C above the long-term average, impacting global rainfall patterns and average temperatures.
That would make this year’s weather event the largest since at least 1950, and possibly since the 19th century, according to the national forecaster.
Other climate groups have projected temperatures to even reach 4C above average.
![People shelter from the rain under an umbrella, in Westminster, central London (Jonathan Brady/PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/21/00/990ec9f645a61d27f28069304365a5a8Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3MzM5OTI3-2.85612596.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
How will El Niño impact London’s weather?
The impact of such an event would mean that London, along with all of northwest Europe, would experience wetter and stormier conditions in the coming autumn and early winter.
El Niño can also increase the odds of cold weather late in the winter.
Professor Adam Scaife, head of long-range forecasting at the Met Office, said: “We should be clear that this is an unprecedented event. I have never seen an El Niño signal this intense in our forecasts.”
He added: “If the forecast is accurate – and other forecast systems show similar extreme values – then 2026 will far exceed our recent experience of El Niño and its worldwide climate influences.”
The Met Office said that El Niño events also drive an increase in global average temperature, with 2027 “very likely” to be the hottest year on record.
Met Office Science Fellow Dr Nick Dunstone said: “During large El Niño events significantly more heat is released from the ocean to the atmosphere leading to an increase in global average temperature, particularly in the calendar year following the winter peak of the El Niño.
Read More
“Hence, 2027 is very likely to replace 2024 as the warmest year on record and be another year to temporarily exceed plus 1.5C above the pre-industrial period”.
Climate change ‘stress’ is increasing
Professor Stephen Belcher, the Met Office’s chief of science and technology, said: “This summer we have experienced heatwaves across Europe reminding us of the effects of climate change, this large El Niño is a reminder that natural variations in the climate system are also at play, adding to the stresses of climate change.”
The unprecedented string of heatwaves and lack of rainfall meant that England saw the driest July on record, with no meaningful rain in London, putting unprecedented pressure on the capital’s cherished parks and beauty spots.
Almost three-quarters of England and all of Wales have been pushed into drought, putting severe pressure on the water system, wildlife, farmers, emergency services and infrastructure.
Earlier this week, the National Fire Chiefs Council said 1,132 wildfires have now been recorded across England and Wales in 2026 so far – a record high for the amount between January and this time of year.
Following an emergency meeting to discuss the heatwave last week, Prime Minister Andy Burnham warned: “We might be in for a wet autumn and winter straight after this, because of El Nino and some of the issues there, which was reported to Cobra.”
The hard, baked ground could make London more susceptible to flash flooding, Sir Sadiq warned in a post on X.
Forecasters and officials have warned that it could take months of sustained rainfall before rivers, reservoirs and groundwaters are completely replenished.
The National Drought Group has warned that drought conditions could persist into the new year as, despite El Nino, current forecasts do not suggest this autumn will have the amount of rainfall required to drive recovery before December.
summary: An unprecedented El Niño event is expected to bring wetter and stormier conditions to London and northwest Europe in the coming autumn and early winter, potentially increasing the odds of late-winter cold weather. This natural climate variation, combined with severe drought and record heatwaves across England, creates a high risk of flash flooding due to hard, baked ground. Furthermore, the El Niño event is projected to drive global temperatures higher, making 2027 very likely to become the warmest year on record.
key_points: An El Niño event is declared when tropical eastern Pacific sea surface temperatures rise 0.5C above average.
London and northwest Europe are expected to experience wetter and stormier autumn and early winter conditions.
The Met Office projects that 2027 will very likely replace 2024 as the hottest year on record.
Almost three-quarters of England and all of Wales have been pushed into drought following the driest July on record.
Hard, baked ground from the drought makes London and other areas more susceptible to flash flooding.

title: What ULEZ has done for childrenâs lungs should silence its loudest critics | LBC
author: Ruth
content:
What ULEZ has done for childrenâs lungs should silence its loudest critics
Ulez's success must be a call to action to carry on in our efforts to improve the air in the UK, writes London mum and clean air campaigner Ruth.
Good news can be hard to come by, but here it is: scientists have been stunned by how quickly childrenâs lungs have recovered following the implementation of the Ultra Low Emission Zone (ULEZ).
Listen to this article
To parents of asthmatic children in London, of which there are hundreds of thousands, this will come as welcome relief.
Iâve spent many sleepless nights listening to my young son coughing and wheezing, thinking about how we can continue to live in a city as highly polluted as London, feeling powerless to provide an environment for my child that would help alleviate his symptoms.
The Mayor of London was courageous and clear-sighted in persevering with the ULEZ, and he deserves credit and praise. This study, which shows how childrenâs lung growth accelerated with cleaner air, has proven that it was worth it. Cleaner air benefits the most vulnerable in our city: children, who deserve the best chance to grow up healthy and unhindered by preventable illness.
It is so worrying to know that the air your child is breathing every day is having a negative impact on their health. Imagine pouring a glass of water from the kitchen tap and knowing that itâs making your family sick, we wouldn't tolerate that.Â Dirty air impacts every organ and is now linked to 700 different illnesses and diseases. The body of evidence is overwhelming and grows every year.
Now we know clearly that clean air measures work, so perhaps we can see this as a call to action to continue our efforts to improve the air in the UK.
Let's bear in mind that whilst we are breathing cleaner air since ULEZ, our air is certainly not meeting World Health Organisation guidelines by quite some way.
There is still work to be done - but as we can see from the results of the CHILL study, this work will surely be worth it. We need a reduction in road transport pollution, action on diesel cars and vans, cheaper, better and more accessible public transport, a phase-out of non-essential domestic wood burning and School Streets across the country.
This would undoubtedly yield further improvements, not just for childrenâs health but for everyone, as well as reducing the costs to the NHS, losses in productivity and quality of life -Â estimated to be at least Â£27 billion for 2025, by the Royal College of Physicians.
____________________
Ruth is a Campaigner at Mums for Lungs.
LBC Opinion provides a platform for diverse opinions on current affairs and matters of public interest.
The views expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the official LBC position.
To contact us emailÂ opinion@lbc.co.uk
summary: Scientists have been stunned by how quickly children's lungs have recovered and accelerated in growth following the implementation of London's Ultra Low Emission Zone (ULEZ). Clean air campaigner and London mother Ruth praises the Mayor of London for persevering with the policy, noting that dirty air is linked to hundreds of illnesses. She argues that this success should serve as a call to action to continue improving air quality across the UK through measures like reducing road transport pollution and expanding public transport.
key_points: Children's lungs have quickly recovered and lung growth has accelerated following the implementation of the ULEZ.
Dirty air impacts every organ and is linked to 700 different illnesses and diseases.
Despite improvements, London's air does not yet meet World Health Organisation guidelines.
Further actions needed include tackling diesel vehicles, improving public transport, phasing out domestic wood burning, and implementing School Streets.
