title: I went to London’s brand new Peaky Blinders experience – this is what it’s like
author: Andrzej Lukowski
content:
[title]
It’s a testament to the endless iconographic appeal of Steven Knight’s Brummie gangland drama that Peaky Blinders: Underworld isn’t even the first immersive Peaky Blinders experience to run in London – that honour went to Peaky Blinders: The Rise, a show so awful I prayed the Shelby gang would drag me out of it and shoot me dead.
Peaky Blinders: Underworld is a very different, greatly improved kettle of fish which doesn’t even use the word ‘immersive’ in its marketing, although to all intents and purposes that’s what it is. (To be clear, it’s made by completely different people, being attributed to the rather inscrutable ‘KMJ Entertainment in partnership with Banijay Rights’).
Made with the blessing of show creator Steven Knight what’s unusual is the fact that Underworld is divided into two sections, one of which is free. Or free-ish: it’s a pub. You don’t have to pay entry to be admitted to The Garrison, which is nominally a recreation of the Victorian boozer that serves as the Shelby gang’s HQ in the show. But to be clear, the pints are very definitely not 1920s prices (that would be about 2p a go).
![Peaky Blinders: Underworld, 2026](https://media.timeout.com/images/106438490/image.webp) 
Built into the London Bridge arches in what I believe is the old location of Southwark Playhouse, I found The Garrison a slightly weird concept: you can’t faithfully magic up an historic pub just like that. It is ultimately a Peaky Blinders theme pub. Still, I wouldn’t rule out a casual pint here if I was in the area: it’s spacious, the period details are clearly faux but for the most part atmospheric rather than tacky (wooden boards, wooden bar, proper barstool, costumed barstaff), and it happily continues the show’s anachronistic music policy with Nick Cave et al on the jukebox and live bands playing several nights a week. There’s also the odd actor barking at us in an enjoyably flinty Brummie accent, although you won’t really get any story in this bit.
The question, then, is whether or not to step into the Underworld, which is the immersive experience behind the pub. Presumably most punters will in fact have prepaid, but I’d assume it’s possible that after a few pints a casual Garrison punter might find themselves spontaneously signing up for the experience.
The pints are very definitely not 1920s prices
Behind the doors, then, is a polished immersive walkthrough area that boils the Birmingham of the show down to its lurid highlights: the fairground; Chinatown; the bookies; the tattoo parlour that is also a bar – that sort of thing. I was given what I’m going to call an activity book upon entry, which has little tokens that enable you to claim a go on each of the fairground games (hook a duck, that sort of thing), plus you can also take on one (or I think more) of several bigger challenges, though on the opening night the only one available was ‘Catch the Rat’, which as you can probably imagine had little to do with rodent control. Although the task was given to me by another appreciably hard-nosed, hard-accented Blinders gang member, the actual job required following clues and solving puzzles in a way that presumably has little bearing on how one actually catches a rat. No rats were harmed in the making of this show. It’s gentle puzzle solving, basically, though the good news is I won a drinks voucher for completing it (I’m not clear if every winner does so).
![Peaky Blinders: Underworld, 2026](https://media.timeout.com/images/106438497/image.webp) 
I think the key things to bear in mind here are that one, the Underworld isn’t particularly massive – you can’t lose yourself in it like a Punchdrunk show – and two, you’re not really getting a great story, just a fairly standard immersive theatre/escape room-style puzzle chain. But it goes about it in a very fun, very atmospheric, very nicely designed way, and if you love that Blinders iconography via the medium of a well-crafted immersive set with some modest lateral thinking thrown in, then it should do it for you. Tickets are around £25 for a one-hour timeslot - some might consider that a bit steep for pottering around a few rooms, but if you get into the quest and are game for the games you’ll have a diverting time (and the prospect of winning a drink takes the edge off the price a bit).
The dirty secret is that obviously nobody – well, almost nobody – really wants to go back to 1920s Birmingham to work for a criminal gang and that is not what Underworld is offering. It’s an opportunity to sink a few tankards, play a few games and be barked at by some impassive Brummie gangsters. If that’s your idea of a good day out then you’ve just found your new favourite London destination.
Peaky Blinders: Underworld is at the London Bridge Arches, just off Tooley St.
Get the latest and greatest from the Big Smoke – from news and reviews to events and trends. Just follow our Time Out London WhatsApp channel.
Stay in the loop: sign up for our free Time Out London newsletter for the best of the city, straight to your inbox.
summary: Peaky Blinders: Underworld is a new immersive experience located in the London Bridge arches, created with the blessing of show creator Steven Knight. It is divided into two sections: a free-to-enter themed pub called The Garrison and a ticketed, one-hour immersive walkthrough area featuring sets, games, and puzzles. While it does not offer a deep narrative, the experience delivers a fun, atmospheric, and nicely designed outing for fans of the show's iconography.
key_points: The experience is located in the London Bridge arches in the former Southwark Playhouse space.
The Garrison is a spacious, themed Victorian-style pub with free entry and live music, though drinks are modern-priced.
The ticketed Underworld section costs around £25 for a one-hour timeslot and features fairground games, themed rooms, and gentle puzzle solving.
Participants can win drinks vouchers by completing challenges like the 'Catch the Rat' puzzle.
The attraction is produced by KMJ Entertainment in partnership with Banijay Rights with Steven Knight's blessing.

title: The world’s first Underground railway is in London and it’s opening to the public for only six days – where you can explore the original 1863 Underground station and its secret tunnels
author: Vaishnavi Pandey
content:
![baker street underground station](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/20111948/42328756044_71c25a87b8_b-2-1024x683.jpg) 
London is home to the world’s first underground railway, and this September you can step inside a closed‑off piece of that history on a special Hidden London tour at a station that helped launch the entire network.
The world’s first underground railway is opening its doors to the public next month
![Baker Street Tube Station, London](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/18174453/Baker-Street-Tube-Station-London-1024x664.jpg)
Opened on 10 January 1863 as part of the Metropolitan Railway, this stop was the launchpad for the idea of carrying passengers beneath Victorian London’s congested streets.
The original “Met” cut a 90‑minute surface journey down to around 20 minutes underground, revolutionising travel in the city and setting the template for metro systems worldwide.
Today, it’s a busy interchange with 10 platforms and five Underground lines, but parts of the station have been hidden from the public for decades.
Baker Street is now famous for its Sherlock Holmes associations, but its real claim to global fame is being part of the world’s first underground railway.
On the tour, you’ll explore original sections of the 1863 station and later Victorian additions, seeing how the space evolved from a single Metropolitan Railway platform into today’s sprawling interchange.
What the Hidden London tour includes
![](https://offloadmedia.feverup.com/secretldn.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/20111333/Underground_Pioneer_at_Baker_Street_-_geograph.org_.uk_-_3305255-1024x683.jpg)
The London Transport Museum’s “The World’s First Underground” tour takes you into areas normally closed to the public, including:
- Original platforms and disused lift shafts
- Corridors last accessed by the public in 1945
- Spaces that once served as Operational Headquarters for London Underground
Over about 85 minutes, guides walk you through 160 years of the station’s story: from the earliest days of Victorian steam‑powered underground travel to the modern multi‑line hub it is today.
You’ll hear what the first passengers thought of travelling underground in 1863, how the network expanded over the next 16 decades, and how the station functioned not just for commuters but for staff who worked (and sometimes played) there.
When you can go visit the world’s first Underground in September
According to the museum’s listing, this tour runs on selected dates through late September, with specific “six days in September” often highlighted in promotional copy. Recent schedules show tour days including:
- Friday 6 September
- Saturday 7 September
- Sunday 8 September
- Wednesday 11 September
- Thursday 12 September
- Friday 13 September
Because slots are limited and the tour is popular, it’s best to check the London Transport Museum’s “Hidden London – Baker Street” page for the exact September dates and availability before planning your visit.
Tickets cost around £45 (£42 concessions), plus a small booking fee. Ticket price also includes half‑price one‑day entry to the London Transport Museum within a month of your tour, and 10% off full‑priced items in the museum shop.
For anyone interested in London’s transport history, Victorian engineering, or simply seeing a side of the city few ever get to, it’s a rare, time‑limited opportunity.
summary: London's Baker Street station, part of the world's first underground railway opened in 1863, is offering rare public tours of its hidden Victorian areas this September. Organized by the London Transport Museum, the 85-minute "Hidden London" tours give visitors access to disused platforms, historic lift shafts, and old operational headquarters normally closed to the public. Tickets cost around £45 and include additional perks like half-price museum entry.
key_points: Baker Street station opened on January 10, 1863, as part of the world's first underground railway.
Special Hidden London tours run for selected days in September, lasting about 85 minutes.
Tours include access to original platforms, disused lift shafts, and corridors last accessed by the public in 1945.
Tickets cost approximately £45 and include half-price entry to the London Transport Museum and a 10% shop discount.

title: Opinion: Why the 'Stranger Things' stars are all headed for the London stage | London Theatre
author: Marianka Swain
content:
Never mind the Upside Down: the new realm that the former residents of Hawkins, Indiana, can’t resist exploring is London theatre. It has just been announced that Noah Schnapp, who played Will Byers on the Netflix sci-fi hit Stranger Things, will make his world stage debut this autumn in Affluenza at the Riverside Studios – and he’s far from the only one.
Sadie Sink, who played Max Mayfield on Stranger Things, was instrumental in turning John Proctor Is the Villain into a Broadway sensation, and has recently crossed the pond too, starring opposite Noah Jupe in Robert Icke’s West End production of Romeo and Juliet. Meanwhile co-star Gaten Matarazzo (aka Dustin Henderson) will star in a major West End revival of RENT from September.
It’s not a crazy transition, since the show itself came to the London stage in the form of the phenomenal Stranger Things: The First Shadow. But it’s fascinating to see the cast now doing the same. So, just why is theatre proving so attractive to the Stranger Things kids?
It’s a completely different world
Being part of a smash-hit global franchise is both a blessing and a curse. The Stranger Things cast became instant stars when the show premiered in 2016, and the series has only grown more popular since: for season four, Netflix reported 140.7 million views in the first 91 days. It changed the lives of a young actors like Matarazzo (13 when Stranger Things kicked off), Sink (14), and Schnapp (just 11).
That level of fame and success is of course thrilling, and can give actors enormous freedom in terms of what projects they pursue next. However, they also have a major challenge to overcome: how to separate themselves from the beloved characters they spent a decade inhabiting on the show.
Many young stars choose to take on completely different work, to demonstrate their range – and all the better if they step into a new world, like theatre. Notably, Daniel Radcliffe did a West End production of Equus at the height of Harry Potter mania. Now the Stranger Things kids are following suit, choosing exciting new roles and shows – and in a completely separate medium to streaming TV – in which to take their all-important post-Stranger Things steps.
Speaking about Affluenza, a thought-provoking new drama set in the ultra-wealthy social haven of the Hamptons, Schnapp noted that he wanted to be “very intentional about what I took on next”, and added that he was excited to “get to play two very different roles” in the play. He’ll be able to demostrate that there’s much more to him than Will Byers.
It’s a great way of growing up
Another difficulty for successful young actors is convincing the world that they’re no longer the cute kids we fell in love with – and that’s definitely the case for the Stranger Things cast. The image of this little gang of friends, cycling through the suburbs together or playing Dungeons & Dragons, is particularly indelible, and although the characters did age on the show, they were all still pretty youthful in the finale.
It’s a canny move, then, to take on much more adult subject matter in your next project, and to do it in a highly respected milieu like London theatre. Both the shows themselves and the locale suggest performers who are maturing and deserve to be taken seriously. Plus there’s nowhere to hide onstage, so it’s a proper test of them as fully-fledged, committed thespians.
Schnapp, as Sink did with John Proctor Is the Villain, is putting his star power behind a new play – a particularly admirable choice. Affluenza deals with provocative contemporary themes like family legacy, moral accountability, and the American justice system. It’s all a far cry from the coming-of-age (and monster fighting) storytelling of Stranger Things – and from its nostalgic 1980s setting.
Sink also impressed by tackling an iconic Shakespearean role, while Matarazzo – who actually has a long-established musical theatre background, with Broadway shows including Les Misérables and Sweeney Todd – is likewise starring in the revival of a classic work. He is playing struggling documentary-maker Mark Cohen in RENT, a show that tackles important, still-resonant topics such as sexuality and queer acceptance, AIDS, gentrification, grief, political protest, and the meaning of art.
It’s an escape from the Hollywood spotlight
While there is, naturally, a lot of excitement around the Stranger Things stars coming to the London stage, it’s a different kind of pressure to working in Hollywood. There is certainly less commercial expectation – particularly for someone like Schnapp, who is doing his show at the independent off-West End venue Riverside Studios – and so perhaps a sense of liberation.
These actors can take chances and experiment without an entire franchise riding on the success of their work. They might discover a new passion – Schnapp is doing theatre for the very first time – or get a sense of where they’d like their career to go next, whether a mix of new and classical stage drama in Sink’s case, or, for Matarazzo, maybe tackling more canonical musical theatre roles like Mark in RENT. They can also experience working in a completely new city, or indeed country.
The London theatre scene is known to be a warm and welcoming community, accepting any artists who are passionate about drama and want to give it their all. The same will doubtless be true for the Stranger Things cast as they seize the opportunity and tackle these bold next projects. After all, there’s no day but today!
Photo credit: Gaten Matarazzo, Sadie Sink, Noah Schnapp. (Photos by Victoria Stevens, Caitlin Cronenberg, and courtesy of Riverside Studios)
summary: Several former stars of the hit series Stranger Things—including Noah Schnapp, Sadie Sink, and Gaten Matarazzo—are transitioning to the London theatre scene for their post-show projects. This move allows the young actors to escape intense Hollywood franchise pressure, distance themselves from their childhood roles, and prove their range with more mature material. By tackling diverse theatrical works, they can demonstrate their growth as serious performers in a welcoming new environment.
key_points: Noah Schnapp will make his world stage debut this autumn in Affluenza at London's Riverside Studios.
Sadie Sink and Gaten Matarazzo are also taking on major roles in London productions, including Romeo and Juliet and RENT.
Transitioning to theatre helps young actors distance themselves from their iconic, long-running characters and demonstrate their acting range.
London theatre offers a different kind of pressure and a sense of liberation compared to the commercial expectations of Hollywood franchises.

title: Major King's Cross rail disruption after person hit by train - live
author: Tom Place; Megan Howe; Niva Yadav
content:

Several London rail services are seriously disrupted after a person was hit by a train.
The incident has shut lines between London and Stevenage and is expected to cause major disruption until 4pm, according to National Rail.
Operators affected include Thameslink, Lumo, LNER and Grand Central Rail.
Later on Thursday, a second person was hit by a train between Farnborough Main and Woking. All lines between these stations have been closed and disruption to services is expected until 7pm.
The Windrush line is not running between Surrey Quays and New Cross, according to TfL.
If you've been affected by what happened on the network today, there is always someone to talk to. You can contact the Samaritans on 116 123 from any phone for a confidential chat.
Scroll down for the latest updates...

Minor delays on the Hammersmith and City line
There are minor delays on the Hammersmith and City line due to train cancellations.
Lines reopen between Finsbury Park and Welwyn Garden City
Lines have reopened between Finsbury Park and Welwyn Garden City
Services will be subject to residual disruption, and passengers have been advised to allow at least 45 minutes extra to complete their journey.
As a result of alterations and cancellations, passengers will likely need to travel on a different train to normal, or change trains at an intermediate station to complete your journey.
You are strongly advised to check journey planners before you travel. If you're travelling now, you should check station screens and listen to announcements for the latest information.
Minor delays on the Central line
Minor delays are affecting the Central line due to a points failure at White City.
Lines reopen between London King's Cross and Stevenage
The emergency services have now completed their work following an earlier incident where a person was hit by a train.

Major disruption is expected until 5pm.

Long distance and mainline South Western Railway services between Exeter St Davids and London Waterloo are currently disrupted.
Some services will be delayed while others may be cancelled or revised.

• Reading and London Paddington
• Basingstoke and Reading
• Exeter and London Paddington
• Weymouth and Westbury

A second person has been hit by a train.
The incident happened between Farnborough Main and Woking.

Trains operating between these stations may be cancelled, delayed by up to 15 minutes or revised.

Lines between London King's Cross and Stevenage, and between Farnborough Main and Woking, faced closures and major delays while emergency services responded. Other routes, including sections of the London Underground and National Rail networks, also encountered issues due to track safety inspections, train faults, and cancellations.
key_points: Lines between London King's Cross and Stevenage reopened following an incident where a person was hit by a train, though residual delays continued.
A second person was struck by a train between Farnborough Main and Woking, closing all lines until evening.
Several operators including Thameslink, Lumo, LNER, Grand Central, and South Western Railway experienced major disruptions.
Minor delays affected the Hammersmith and City, Central, and Metropolitan underground lines due to cancellations and a points failure.
Additional disruptions were reported on Gatwick Express and Southern routes due to a train fire and a track safety inspection.

title: Inside London's illegal rave renaissance
author: Mattha Busby
content:
![Inside London's illegal rave renaissance](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/20/9/57/Illegal-raves.jpeg?trim=164,0,38,0&quality=100&auto=webp&width=1920)
Inside London's illegal rave renaissance
Secret networks are keeping the capital’s free parties alive
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
On Saturday nights around 11pm, hundreds of young Londoners gather at train stations and in car parks after the first location — or “loco” — drops into an encrypted group chat. An hour or two later, they’re dancing inside abandoned office blocks, shuttered restaurants and empty warehouses as generators hum and bass reverberates through buildings long forgotten by the city.
By 3am, there might be 2,000 people inside — more than many licensed clubs can legally hold. Sometimes police stand outside while organisers invoke squatters’ rights. Sometimes they never arrive at all. The conventional night out might be dying a slow death, but the free party movement is thriving, whether inside London or in fields, forests or barns outside the city. Forget the polished, Instagram-friendly sound dominating much of today’s club scene. The music you’ll hear at these parties will span donk, psytrance, techno and tekno, a raw, fast-paced electronic music genre born out of the free party movement.
“It’s clearly growing in a way that it hasn’t done for a while,” says Aaron Trinder, the director of Free Party: A Folk History. “I think that’s down to the lack of an alternative for people.”
Spiralling ticket prices, widespread venue closures and increasingly heavy-handed security have pushed some young Londoners away from licensed nightlife and towards illegal parties, where entry is often little more than a suggested £5-10 donation. In return, many say they recover something missing from conventional clubbing: freedom. And a can of Stella for £2.50.
“For young partygoers, going to a club has become increasingly challenging, and that’s why the free party scene has started bubbling again,” says Alessandro Ugo, the director of F[r]EE: Behind the Scenes of the Free Party Culture. “Free parties are self-managed, you are part of the party. How you behave affects the vibe.”
Photographer Yushy has attended more than 150 unlicensed parties over the past five years and last year published his book, Section 63: Documenting Underground London Raves. He found a scene largely hostile to social media — and to documentation more generally. That means people are more likely to be immersed in the moment and less concerned about appearances.
“I could look at somebody who was completely different to me and think, we made it into this together,” he says. “We waited two or three hours for the location, we ran away from the police, but we’re here together as one unit.”
On one occasion, he recalls partying in a former Gordon Ramsay restaurant in central London. “There were about 200 or 300 people there raving and we could just see Leicester Square underneath us,” he says. “People were just sitting in booths talking to each other while drum and bass played.” After years of partying in abandoned buildings across the capital, he came away convinced of “how empty London really is”.
The scene also attracts opportunists seeking to disrupt the convivial fun — selling balloons and substandard drugs, stealing phones and escalating conflicts.
A well-known sound system crew organised a party, London’s Calling Vol. 2, which was attended by a few thousand opposite the closed Printworks club in Rotherhithe at the beginning of this year, but they vowed never to do so in the capital again. “Many of our crew and staff were assaulted, had weapons pulled on them, and some were hospitalised while trying to keep everyone safe,” they said in a statement circulated on Telegram. “The same problem has followed London parties for years now: people turning up with pathetic rivalries, egos, weapons, bringing street politics into spaces that are meant to be about music and freedom.”
But the party will go on, whether inside the capital or not, even as organisers risk punishment and larger parties are less common as they are more likely to get busted with the advent of the internet.
In 1994, John Major’s government made free parties illegal but the burgeoning acid house scene largely found a home in licensed venues. Now history has come full circle after interest surged after the pandemic.
“There will always be a newer, younger generation with enough courage to say, ‘OK, I’m gonna start a crew, squat that building and start throwing parties’,” says Ugo. Despite the risks, the movement is no longer as marginal as it once seemed.
The annual Night Time Industries Association report in February reported on an underground resurgence, with free parties and unlicensed raves numbering about 1,350 parties per year — roughly four per cent of all UK electronic music events.
The essence of a free party, however, cannot be manufactured. What keeps people coming back is something that cannot easily be commercialised.
“In a free party you feel more welcome, you feel you’re part of a community,” says Ugo. “Many people think ‘free’ means free of charge, but a free party is free in your mind.”
summary: London is experiencing a resurgence of illegal raves and free parties as young people seek alternatives to traditional, costly, and heavily secured licensed nightlife. Driven by encrypted group chats, thousands gather in abandoned spaces to listen to genres like tekno and techno. While the scene offers a sense of community, freedom, and affordability, it also faces challenges such as police intervention, safety risks, and occasional violence.
key_points: Unlicensed free parties in London are thriving due to spiralling ticket prices, venue closures, and heavy-handed club security.
Parties are organized via encrypted group chats, drawing crowds of up to 2,000 people to abandoned office blocks, warehouses, and empty restaurants.
The underground scene numbers about 1,350 parties per year across the UK, according to a Night Time Industries Association report.
While participants value the immersion and community spirit, organizers sometimes contend with violence, weapons, and opportunists disrupting events.

title: The 6 best free things to do in London this weekend [August 21-23 2026]
author: Alice Saville
content:
[title]
There are a billion and one different things to do in London over the summer. Day festivals, bars, outdoor theatre shows and blockbuster exhibitions are all jostling for attention and competing for your time, and cash. But what happens when September is looming, and your bank account is looking drier than one of Hackney’s drought-stricken canals?
Well, we’ve got an idea or two. We’ve hunted high and low across this city to find free things to do this weekend that are actually worth your time. Spectacular circus acts in the open air. Queer dance parties with the edgiest DJs around. Joyful street parties with live music. Don’t let the fun run out when the funds run out. Read on for our pick of the very best events to enjoy, without getting your bankcard out.
The best free things on in London this weekend, August 21-23 2026
In a city where free theatre is harder to come by than an outdoor table at Towpath Cafe, Greenwich Fair is an annual miracle. It takes over the summit of Greenwich Park for a weekend of outdoor shows that play across multiple stages, with roving performers working the crowd. No need to book: just turn up, find a seat, and discover anything from feminist high-wire act ElevateHer by Daughters of the Wire, to Kismat Walla by Thingumajig Theatre, a magical outdoor puppetry show inspired by South Asian street markets.
Greenwich Park, Park Row, SE10 8XJ. Sat Aug 22 - Sun Aug 23. Free.
![Caspian’s Storm, Greenwich Fair, 2026](https://media.timeout.com/images/106426191/image.webp) 
It’s been a big old summer of LGBTQ+ partying, with Pride, Mighty Hoopla, and Body Movements all pulling fun-loving crowds of revellers. Now, it’s time to head east and enjoy one of the last massive get-togethers of this year’s queer calendar: and thankfully for everyone’s bank balance, it’s totally free. Queer Frequencies is the latest in the series of free parties that began with The Music Is Ours back in June. It’s a party that’ll put Black queer music and culture front and centre , with a line-up curated by DJ Shy One, ‘the Prince of Peckham’ Mark-Ashley Dupé, east London creative Donnie Sunshine and DJ Joel Mignott. Head on over to Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park for an afternoon of dancing and discovering new acts in the late August sunshine.
Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, E20 2ST. Sat Aug 22 - Sun Aug 23. Free.
Arts Emergency is a charity that’s dedicated to making sure the next generation of creatives find their way into the spotlight, even as schools cut art, music, theatre and literature out of the curriculum. Get a feel for what they do at this exciting two-day takeover at Southbank Centre. On Saturday, you’ll find loads of ways to get moving, with workshops by dance groups Strut, Queer Salsa, and Polyjammerous. Then on Sunday, there’s a one-off edition of storytelling open mic night Special Guest, where actors, writers and comedians tell stories inspired by words from the audience, backed up by a live band.
Southbank Centre, Belvedere Road, SE1 8XX. Sat Aug 22 - Sun Aug 23. Free.
![Pinterest](https://media.timeout.com/images/106437371/image.webp) 
Delight your friends and befuddle your enemies by getting some sparkling face gems at Pinterest’s Mile End pop-up, which is all about getting festival-ready. You’ll also be able to pick up e.l.f. cosmetics and learn how to use them from the pros, as well as getting your mitts on customisable single use cameras and festival merch. And if the ‘festival’ you’re going to is your very un-Pinterest-worthy disposable BBQ in your mate’s arid backyard? Don't worry, we won’t tell ‘em if you don’t.
All Time Food and Wine, 564 Mile End Road, E3 4PH. Sat Aug 22. Free.
Ridley Road Market is never quiet, but this Saturday it’s going to be buzzing to a different frequency thanks to its annual summer party. From noon, it’ll be soundtracked by the sweet sounds of steel pan bands, sound systems and African drumming workshops. There’ll also be face painting for the kids, a free photobooth, fun interactive games to try – and of course, loads of delicious food from Ridley Road’s many traders.
Ridley Road Market, E8. Sat Aug 22. Free.
![Buzz Gym’s Soca dance class](https://media.timeout.com/images/106438448/image.webp) 
Bored of punishing 5k runs or tedious weight-training? Try a fun new form of exercise at this free Wembley Park workshop, which will introduce you to the joys of Caribbean Soca dancing. Buzz Gym will lead you through an hour of fast-paced, rhythmic movement that'll send you beaming into the rest of your Sunday.
Union Park, Wembley Park. Sun Aug 23. Free.
Make the most of August with our guide to the best things to do in London this month.
Get the latest and greatest from the Big Smoke – from news and reviews to events and trends. Just follow our Time Out London WhatsApp channel.
Stay in the loop: sign up for our free Time Out London newsletter for the best of the city, straight to your inbox.
summary: London offers several free events and activities for the weekend of August 21-23, 2026, helping residents enjoy the city despite diminishing summer funds. Highlights include outdoor circus performances at Greenwich Park, a Black queer music party at Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, and a two-day creative takeover at the Southbank Centre. Additional free experiences feature a festival pop-up in Mile End, a lively summer party at Ridley Road Market, and a Soca dance class in Wembley Park.
key_points: Greenwich Fair features free outdoor shows, high-wire acts, and puppetry at Greenwich Park on August 22-23.
Queer Frequencies hosts a free celebration of Black queer music and culture at Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park.
The Southbank Centre hosts a two-day Arts Emergency takeover with dance workshops and a storytelling open mic night.
Pinterest and e.l.f. cosmetics are running a free festival-ready pop-up at Mile End on Saturday, August 22.
Ridley Road Market's annual summer party offers steel pan bands, African drumming, and games on Saturday, August 22.

title: Oxford Street pedestrianisation works to start next month
author: Ian Mansfield
content:
Oxford Street pedestrianisation works to start next month
Work to ban vehicles from a large section of Oxford Street is set to start next month, when the first major construction work gets underway.
![](https://www.ianvisits.co.uk/articles/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/oxford-street.jpg)
Subject to the necessary approvals, works will commence on 2 September 2026, and Oxford Street between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street should be traffic-free by mid to late October. That’s basically from Selfridges in the west through to just past Oxford Circus in the east.
During construction, tube and rail services will continue to operate normally, although some bus routes will be temporarily diverted or altered as the road changes are introduced. Taxis and private hire vehicles will also continue to operate in the area, but some existing pick-up and drop-off points may have to move.
One of the more complicated aspects of removing traffic from Oxford Street will be maintaining access for the hundreds of shops, restaurants and other businesses that need regular deliveries, waste collections and servicing. Ahead of the traffic restrictions coming into effect, TfL is holding online and in-person sessions with businesses to explain how deliveries and servicing will operate once Oxford Street becomes traffic-free.
The September works are the first major physical changes associated with the pedestrianisation plans, although the initial traffic-free street will not be the finished scheme.
The longer-term plans envisage a substantial redesign of Oxford Street as a pedestrian-focused public space, but the immediate priority is removing through traffic from the section between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street.
If the construction programme runs to schedule, traffic should disappear from this central stretch of Oxford Street by mid to late October. Just in time for the Christmas lights to go up.
summary: Construction work to pedestrianise a major section of Oxford Street is scheduled to begin on September 2, 2026, subject to approvals. The area between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street is expected to be traffic-free by mid to late October. This initial phase focuses on removing through traffic ahead of a longer-term public space redesign.
key_points: Construction work begins on September 2, 2026, subject to approvals.
The affected section spans from Orchard Street to Great Portland Street.
The area is expected to be traffic-free by mid to late October 2026.
Tube and rail services will operate normally, while some bus routes and taxi points will be altered.
TfL is engaging with local businesses regarding deliveries and servicing logistics.

title: Omaze launches £3.5million north London house prize draw
author: Megan Howe
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Omaze launches £3.5million north London Victorian house prize draw](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/19/20/53/Copy-of-H54_London_VII_KEYES_ROAD_OUTSIDE_DINING_01-V4_HighRes_16x9.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
A stunning Victorian family home is up for grabs in a prize draw raising funds for the London Air Ambulance Charity.
The winner of the Omaze Million Pound House Draw London — which is being backed by Rita Ora— will get the keys to a five-bedroom period home in Mapesbury, north London worth £3.5 million along with £250,000 in cash.
The house boasts a number of features, including original stained-glass windows, high ceilings, oak herringbone flooring and an open plan kitchen and dining area with doors leading onto the garden which has a treehouse and zip line.
Set within the Mapesbury Conservation area, which is prized for its leafy streets and period architecture, the property comes mortgage-free, with all stamp duty and legal fees covered, plus £195,000 worth of furnishings.
The winner will also receive £250,000 in cash to help them settle in, and can choose to either move in, rent it out for supplementary income, or sell up to become a cash multi-millionaire.
If they choose to rent it out, estimates suggest the property could achieve a long-term rental value of between £12,000 and £13,000 per month.
![](<https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/19/21/39/Copy-of-H54_London_VII_KEYES_ROAD_DINING_ROOM_01-(1)_HighRes_16x9.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960>)
The ground floor has an entrance hall, spacious lounge, kitchen and dining room, snug, home office and a garage with workshop space. The first floor offers a main bedroom with dressing room and en suite, two further bedrooms and a bathroom, plus a utility room.
The second floor houses two more bedrooms, one dressed as a playroom, and a further bathroom.The grounds stretch to approximately 320ft and include mature trees, Japanese maples and bamboo, alongside a separate contemporary garden studio housing a wellness space with ice baths just outside. There is also private off-street parking for two cars.
The property sits in North West London, close to Mapesbury Dell, a local green space, with Willesden Green and its Jubilee line connections a short walk away, offering routes into central London in around half an hour.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/19/21/41/Copy-of-H54_London_VII_KEYES_ROAD_EXTERIOR_03-V3_HighRes_16x9.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
London’s Air Ambulance Charity’s advanced medical teams are the only ones who can get to a patient in time to make a difference.
Their vehicles can get across the capital in under 11 minutes and their teams are the only ones able to perform hospital-level surgery at scene.
Read More
This includes ECMO, a technique to temporarily take over heart and lung function in patients who don’t respond to standard resuscitation.
Following a successful trial, the transformative funding from Omaze will allow London’s Air Ambulance teams to deliver dedicated ECMO-enabled teams throughout the week and establish these teams in parallel to their existing service for traumatic injury.
![](<https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/19/21/24/Copy-of-H54_London_VII_KEYES_ROAD_ICE_BATH-(1)_HighRes_16x9.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960>)
Rita said: “As a proud Londoner, I’ve been aware of the work of London’s Air Ambulance Charity all my life.
“It is a service for everyone who lives, works and visits our amazing city, and their teams make a transformational difference to thousands of people every year. I couldn’t be prouder to support this service, and now I’m excited that so many other people can too.
“Every person who enters the Omaze Million Pound House Draw can join me in supporting the delivery of their groundbreaking ECAT service, creating a chance for survival for cardiac arrest patients across London and beyond.”
This is the second time Omaze has partnered with London's Air Ambulance Charity.
Sir David Beckham fronted the first campaign in 2024, which raised £4 million to help fund two new helicopters for the life-saving service. The new helicopters have helped London's Air Ambulance Charity reach more patients than ever, with the service recording its busiest ever summer in 2026, averaging seven missions a day - up from its historic high of six.
![](<https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/19/21/25/Copy-of-H54_London_VII_KEYES_ROAD_SNUG-(1)_HighRes_16x9.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960>)
Matt Pohlson, Founder and CEO of Omaze, said: "Everyone at Omaze is delighted to be partnering with London's Air Ambulance Charity again for our latest house draw.“This partnership is especially close to my heart. The new rapid response vehicles we're helping to fund carry an ECMO machine - the very same technology that saved me when I became the recipient of the first ever transfer of one between hospitals. It's remarkable to think that equipment will now be out there saving more people on the streets of London.
"By offering this incredible property in North West London, plus £250,000 in cash, Omaze gives someone the chance to win a truly life-changing prize, while also raising vital funds for London's Air Ambulance Charity's lifesaving work.
"The lucky winner will have several fantastic options available to them - moving into this beautiful home, renting it out for a significant extra income, or selling up to become a cash multi-millionaire. The choice is entirely theirs, and whatever they decide, it will change their lives forever.
"Thanks to the generosity of the Omaze Community, we've now raised well over £150 million for good causes across the UK."
The Grand Prize Draw closes on Sunday 27th September 2026 for online entries and Tuesday 29th September 2026 for postal entries.
summary: Omaze has launched a £3.5 million Victorian house prize draw in Mapesbury, north London, backed by singer Rita Ora to raise funds for the London Air Ambulance Charity. The five-bedroom period property comes mortgage-free with stamp duty, legal fees, £195,000 worth of furnishings, and an additional £250,000 in cash for the winner. The campaign supports the charity's groundbreaking services, including funding dedicated ECMO-enabled teams for cardiac arrest patients.
key_points: The prize is a five-bedroom Victorian family home in Mapesbury, north London, valued at £3.5 million.
The winner receives the house mortgage-free along with £250,000 in cash and £195,000 worth of furnishings.
The prize draw raises funds for the London Air Ambulance Charity and is backed by Rita Ora.
Funding from the draw will help the charity deliver dedicated ECMO-enabled teams for cardiac arrest patients.
The Grand Prize Draw closes on September 27, 2026, for online entries and September 29, 2026, for postal entries.

title: Million Dollar Quartet confirms full London transfer cast
author: Alex Wood
content:
![MDQ 300x200](https://www.whatsonstage.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2026/08/MDQ-300x200-1.png?w=300) 
The production was first seen at the Barn in Cirencester
Full casting has been confirmed for the London transfer of the Barn Theatre’s production of Million Dollar Quartet.
Connor Payne will reprise his performance as Elvis Presley, alongside Christopher Erasmus as Johnny Cash, Joe Bence as Jerry Lee Lewis and Joey Bradick as Carl Perkins. Darren Day, previously announced, returns as record producer Sam Phillips.
They are joined by Jenay Naima as Dyanne, Geraint Downing as Brother Jay and Josh Haberfield as W S “Fluke” Holland. The full London company reprises its roles from the production’s Barn Theatre run.
The musical is set on 4 December 1956, when Presley, Cash, Lewis and Perkins famously came together for an impromptu recording session at Sun Records in Memphis. The score includes songs such as “Blue Suede Shoes”, “Fever”, “Walk the Line” and “Hound Dog”.
Jonathan O’Boyle directs, with choreography by Joanna Goodwin, set and costume design by Libby Watson, lighting design by Alex Musgrave, sound design by Nick Lodge and musical supervision by Lee Freeman. The casting director is Harry Blumenau.
The London engagement follows an extended run at the Barn Theatre in Cirencester and continues the venue’s Built By Barn initiative, following productions including I’m Sorry Prime Minister, I Can’t Quite Remember and the forthcoming UK tour of The King’s Speech.
Iwan Lewis, CEO and artistic director of the Barn Theatre, said: “I’m incredibly proud to bring the entire Barn company of Million Dollar Quartet from the Cotswolds to London. As more of our productions take on a future life, it means so much to continue that journey with the artists who made them a success. This company has blown away audiences at the Barn. Now it’s London’s turn.”
The musical, with a book by Colin Escott and Floyd Mutrux, premiered on Broadway in 2010 before making its West End debut at the Noël Coward Theatre in 2011. It later returned to London as part of a UK tour in 2016 and 2017.
The show runs at The Arts at Marble Arch: powered by TodayTix from 4 September to 6 December 2026, with a press night on 15 September.
summary: Full casting has been confirmed for the London transfer of the Barn Theatre’s production of Million Dollar Quartet. title: 'Heat hell' of London loft conversions: 100,000s face retrofit need in climate crisis
author: Nicholas Cecil
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) ![‘London is cooking’: Sadiq Khan warns London isn't built for 40°C heat as temperatures soared this summer](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/05/07/10/bf747f785d2b3be819fe4306497142b9Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzc4MjMyOTUw-2.75393480.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75) ![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png) Hundreds of thousands of Londoners face having to retrofit their loft conversions as temperatures soar in coming years, a new report is warning. “We must create cooler homes and buildings, greener and shadier neighbourhoods, and infrastructure that can withstand a hotter climate,” Sir Sadiq stressed. Loft conversions have been specifically identified by City Hall as a priority housing type for overheating retrofit. The Heat Ready London Technical Report, commissioned by the Mayor, told how climate-related damage could cost the capital up to £36 billion a year by the 2050s. More than half of homes in Britain already experience overheating risk, it explained. Without adaptation, under a high-emissions warming scenario for 2C warming in 2050, the overheating risk in a typical summer is projected to result in up to 10,000 excess heat-related deaths in the UK. Indoor overheating, the report added, is the primary causal exposure for most heat-related premature deaths and ill-health. “With 92 per cent of residents in all existing homes affected by heat risk, it is critical homes are retrofitted to be heat-resilient,” the study said. Highlighting the varied housing stock across London, it added: “Some archetypes such as top-floor flats, loft conversions, bungalows and highly insulated and glazed homes have higher risk of overheating. “The variation in stock requires a flexible approach to retrofit, which allows for a diversity of solutions to be implemented.” ![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/19/15/01KSMNC82RMJXFWK22YW88BZHN.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) The report proposes that loft conversions are included in a wider programme to retrofit London's highest-risk homes. Read More Measures which could be used include: * Shutters * Ceiling fans * External shading * Improved ventilation * Solar-controlled window films * In some cases active cooling/air conditioning * Secure purge ventilation to rapidly remove air or pollutants * Insulation designed as part of an overheating strategy ![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/19/18/01K7K75MHGQR51CSV7HHZDEHZ4.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) Hundreds of thousands of Londoners have extended their homes upwards, with loft conversions, over the years. The trend was fuelled by soaring house prices in the capital, and partly by rises in stamp duty imposed by former Chancellor George Osborne more than a decade ago on more costly properties, which made it more expensive for some people to move in parts of London. Many of the new loft rooms have high quality double glazing to keep in the heat during the autumn and winter. But as temperatures are now soaring regularly above 30C during the summer, they are also retaining the heat which rises in homes into the loft area. So, many Londoners now face having to retrofit their loft conversions or put up with unbearable heat in future years. Sir Sadiq said: “The climate crisis is on our doorstep. “It is already threatening Londoners’ lives, disrupting vital services and costing our economy hundreds of millions of pounds. “Without further action, climate change could cost London as much as £36 billion a year by the 2050s.” The report also outlined how lost productivity linked to high temperatures is estimated to cost London £577 million a year. The plan showed how around one million London homes are at risk of overheating, alongside 1,361 schools, 60 hospitals and 351 care homes in areas most vulnerable to extreme heat. It proposed a series of measures including boosting health services to deal with heat incidents, making public transport more resilient, making homes and workplaces cooler, more cooling spaces, trees and public drinking water. The danger to Londoners is not limited to days of extreme heat, the research stressed. About 90 per cent of heat-related deaths in London happen when temperatures are between 24°C and 32°C. Evidence also suggests Londoners aged between 45 and 65 face a greater risk of dying during hot weather than people of the same age nationally. ![

The new Piccadilly line trains

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/06/23/16/30/Picaddillyline.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) Plans for new air-conditioned trains on the Piccadilly line and DLR have been hit by delays.
summary: A new Heat Ready London Technical Report commissioned by the Mayor warns that hundreds of thousands of Londoners will need to retrofit their loft conversions due to severe indoor overheating risks as temperatures rise. The report states that climate-related damage could cost the capital up to £36 billion a year by the 2050s, with indoor overheating serving as the primary cause of heat-related premature deaths. Proposed adaptation measures for at-risk properties include external shading, shutters, improved ventilation, ceiling fans, and solar-controlled window films.
key_points: Hundreds of thousands of Londoners face retrofitting loft conversions because they trap rising heat during soaring summer temperatures.
The Heat Ready London report warns that climate-related damage could cost the capital up to £36 billion annually by the 2050s.
More than half of homes in Britain currently experience overheating risk, which is a primary cause of heat-related premature deaths.
Proposed retrofit solutions include shutters, ceiling fans, external shading, improved ventilation, and solar-controlled window films.

title: Murder probe launched after woman dies in Hounslow house fire
author: Megan Howe
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) ![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/19/20/01M0DQENGP1MEM0AQVAVM5ZG8N.jpg?trim=125,0,125,0&quality=75&auto=webp&width=1000) ![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png) Nine people were taken to hospital with injuries, where a 48-year-old woman later died. Her family have been informed and are being supported by specially trained officers. ![

Police work at a fire damaged property following a fire on Berkeley Avenue in Hounslow in which a 48-year-old woman died and a further eight people were taken to hospital

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/19/20/01M0DR83PT9AXDAQ3CS0WXPWSH.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) Another woman, aged 40, remains in hospital in a life-threatening condition. The remaining seven people, six men and one woman, have since been discharged after receiving treatment for minor injuries. Detective Chief Inspector Neil John, who is leading the investigation, said: "Our thoughts are first and foremost with the victim's family and loved ones at this extremely difficult time, as well as everyone who has been injured. ![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/19/20/01M0DR5CF3MG4PYCNTYNQ38X5F.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) "Our enquiries are progressing at pace as we work to establish the full circumstances surrounding the fire, which we believe may have been started deliberately. "We understand this to be an isolated incident within a residential address; however, we understand it will cause concern within the local community. Officers will remain in the area throughout the day, and we will provide updates as our investigation continues. "I would ask anyone with information that could assist our enquiries, including CCTV, doorbell camera or dashcam footage, to contact us." Anyone with information, or footage that may assist the investigation, is urged to contact police on 101, quoting CAD 359/19Aug.
summary: A murder investigation has been launched following a house fire on Berkeley Avenue in Hounslow. Nine people were hospitalized, resulting in the death of a 48-year-old woman and leaving a 40-year-old woman in life-threatening condition. Police believe the fire may have been started deliberately and are appealing for information and footage from the public.
key_points: A 48-year-old woman died after being taken to the hospital from a house fire in Hounslow.
A 40-year-old woman remains hospitalized in a life-threatening condition.
Seven other individuals were treated for minor injuries and have been discharged.
Police suspect the fire may have been started deliberately and are treating the incident as isolated.

title: London paramedics first to use underwater drones, LAS claims
author: Karl Mercer
content:
![Christel Oweis holds the drone in the water. She wears the HART rescue uniform and a yellow hard hat.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/640/cpsprodpb/8a09/live/d005a610-9bd0-11f1-bb4d-1147ef2e78e5.jpg)
The drone is used alongside sonar to find and retrieve casualties underwater
- Published
In the Lee Valley White Water Centre, London's specialist paramedics from the Hazardous Area Response Team are training with their new kit.
They recently purchased three unmanned underwater vehicles - known as underwater drones - that can be used in the search and rescue of people who have got into difficulty in water.
"It's the best," said Sam Barton, from the London Ambulance Service (LAS). "[We are] the first ambulance service in the country to have this piece of kit and one of the first emergency services as well."
The drones enter the water and use a mechanical grabber arm to rescue casualties from dangerous water conditions. Previously, paramedics used long-armed poles to try to reach casualties safely.
The Hazardous Area Response Team come to the Lee Valley White Water Centre every year to refresh their skills. They also carry out white-water training in north Wales once a year.
Barton explains how the drone works: "We've got eight motors to keep it nice and stable in the water and move it through the water. We can go up and down, side to side, and we've got two really bright lights to allow us to see underwater."
Barton said the drone also had a camera at the front which sends a live image to the controller, and an arm that can grab hold of a casualty.
It is deployed alongside sonar technology the team have been using for the past few years to locate casualties under the surface.
![The drone with its lights on, is on display on the shore.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/640/cpsprodpb/c4d3/live/ed761e00-9bd0-11f1-bb4d-1147ef2e78e5.jpg)
The drone uses eight motors and a grabber arm when it is under water
Paramedic Christel Oweis explains how the device uses echo location to identify items in the water.
"I go underwater and it sends out a little ping as I do a scan. If that ping hits anything, it will bounce back and the sonar device will receive an echo," she said.
"It will then use AI to analyse that echo, and if it could be a person it will show an 'X' on the screen."
Once a person and their location are identified, the drone, which is attached to a line on the shore, is deployed.
During the training exercise, it was sent out to retrieve a realistic dummy, which the team had weighed down in the water.
Oweis said the drone allowed them to search for, locate, and rescue casualties "really quickly".
"All our HART (Hazardous Area Response Teams) paramedics are trained to perform rescues in fast-flowing water and still water, however it can be quite dangerous," she said.
"[The drone] can be deployed in less than two minutes."
Of the three underwater drones owned by LAS, one is used for training and two are in operation, one in east London and the other in west London.
Barton said the new technology was helping their teams, particularly in the summer when the risks of the capital's waterways increase in hot weather.
The specialist paramedic explained that when water temperatures were higher, crews had less time to rescue someone from drowning, due to the way the body's organs continued to operate when submerged.
Conversely, in water under 6C, the cold water rapidly cools the brain. When cold, the brain requires less oxygen and it can tolerate the lack of blood flow for a much longer period.
Barton said this meant that in cooler water, their team had about 90 minutes to complete a rescue, compared to 30 minutes when the water was warmer.
This time limit refers to complete submersion and not the immediate dangers of cold water shock and hypothermia that can also occur in cold water.
"It's absolutely imperative that we can get this [drone] in the water as quickly as possible to try and rescue as many people as we can," he said.
Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
summary: The London Ambulance Service (LAS) has become the first ambulance service in the country to use underwater drones for water rescue operations. The Hazardous Area Response Team (HART) uses the drones, equipped with sonar, cameras, and mechanical grabber arms, to quickly locate and retrieve casualties from dangerous waters. These tools are especially vital during the summer months when warmer water temperatures significantly reduce the time available to rescue a submerged person.
key_points: The London Ambulance Service is the first ambulance service in the UK to introduce underwater drones for rescues.
The drones feature eight motors, bright lights, a front-facing camera, and a mechanical grabber arm to retrieve casualties.
Sonar technology and AI are used alongside the drones to scan and identify people underwater.
The LAS currently owns three underwater drones: one for training and two operational units deployed in east and west London.
Warmer water temperatures reduce the safe rescue window to 30 minutes, compared to 90 minutes in water under 6C.

title: RIGHT BEFORE I GO. LONDON TRANSFER ANNOUNCED
author: Shaun Tossell
content:
⭐ RIGHT BEFORE I GO. LONDON TRANSFER ANNOUNCED ⭐
A London transfer of suicide prevention play RIGHT BEFORE I GO. has been announced.
From Stan Zimmerman (writer of Golden Girls and Gilmore Girls), RIGHT BEFORE I GO. will transfer to London’s Soho Theatre for a limited time following its hit run at Edinburgh Festival Fringe.
A star-studded cast including Iz Hesketh (Tip Toe), Dominique Moore (Horrible Histories), Claire-Marie Hall (Operation Mincemeat), Emrhys Cooper (Nosferatu), Gerard McCarthy (The Fall), Paul Bigley (The Danish Girl) and Tosh Wanogho-Maud (Kinky Boots) will join Stan Zimmerman himself, directed by Abigail Morris.
The suicide awareness play highlights the raw struggles of people from all walks of life that have been impacted by suicide. RIGHT BEFORE I GO. uses real suicide notes of celebrities, veterans, bullied teens, those identifying as LGBTQ+, and those who have survived attempts.
The play is followed by a talkback between the cast, audience and a local mental health professional. September is Suicide Awareness Month, and the play is part of awareness raising activities during the month, including World Suicide Prevention Day on 10th September 2026.
RIGHT BEFORE I GO. has travelled across the USA, including a run in NYC at The Tank, featuring stars including Vanessa Williams, Olly Alexander, Christine Taylor and Patrick Page. At Edinburgh Festival Fringe, Stan Zimmerman was joined by Wendie Malick and Emily Kuroda in a critically acclaimed run. The London transfer is produced by Rodrigo Jorge for Dreamatorium Entertainment, and co-produced by Joan Lane for Wild Thyme Productions.
RIGHT BEFORE I GO. will play Soho Theatre, London, running from 5th – 10th September 2026, with tickets on sale now.
Interesting! ! !
Thoughts? X x x
summary: The suicide prevention play 'Right Before I Go,' written by Stan Zimmerman, is transferring to London's Soho Theatre for a limited run from September 5 to 10, 2026. Following a hit run at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, the production features a star-studded cast and incorporates real suicide notes to highlight the impact of suicide. The performances will be followed by talkbacks involving the cast, audience, and a mental health professional as part of Suicide Awareness Month activities.
key_points: The play 'Right Before I Go' is transferring to London's Soho Theatre for a limited run in September 2026.
It is written by Stan Zimmerman and directed by Abigail Morris, following a successful run at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe.
The production utilizes real suicide notes to explore the struggles of individuals impacted by suicide.
Each performance is followed by a talkback session featuring the cast, audience, and a local mental health professional.
The London run coincides with Suicide Awareness Month and World Suicide Prevention Day.

title: Cheaper e-bikes are coming to south London
author: Eloise Feilden
content:
[title]
Last September Hackney became the first London borough to introduce a game-changing price cap for Lime bikes, making them as cheap as buses. Now, a second borough in the Big Smoke is making trips on e-bikes less spenny.
Residents and key workers in Southwark will benefit from a new deal that the local council has negotiated with three of the biggest e-bike operators. Twenty-minute trips on Lime, Voi and Forest will set riders back a maximum of £1.75. That’s a serious saving, considering that the same ride currently costs as much as £7 a pop if you’re riding pay-as-you-go.
Southwark Council is also cracking down on pavement parking. The e-bike companies have agreed to fund enforcement and reporting channels for residents, so that e-bikes left on pavements can be removed tout de suite. E-bikes in Southwark will also get less noisy, as the agreement includes a clause on electric bike alarms being turned off at night so they cause less disturbance to locals.
![Forest Bike, London](https://media.timeout.com/images/106438162/image.webp) 
A total of 8.2 million e-bike trips were made in Southwark in 2025, with use in the borough increasing by 356 percent over the last two years.
James McAsh, leader of Southwark Council, said the new agreement would be monitored to ‘make sure the deal works for people in Southwark’. He said: ‘It’s vital that people in our borough benefit from e-bikes and also have protections in place to make sure they are used properly.’
Exactly when Southwark’s new e-bike deal for residents and key workers will come into effect is to be confirmed.

summary: Southwark Council has negotiated a new deal with major e-bike operators Lime, Voi, and Forest to cap twenty-minute trips at £1.75 for residents and key workers. The agreement also addresses community concerns by funding enforcement against pavement parking and requiring nighttime bike alarms to be turned off. This follows a massive surge in e-bike usage, with 8.2 million trips recorded in the borough in 2025.
key_points: Southwark is the second London borough to introduce a price cap on e-bikes after Hackney.
Twenty-minute trips with Lime, Voi, and Forest will cost a maximum of £1.75 for residents and key workers.
E-bike operators will fund enforcement and reporting channels to remove bikes parked improperly on pavements.
Electric bike alarms will be turned off at night to reduce noise disturbances for locals.
E-bike use in Southwark increased by 356 percent over the last two years, reaching 8.2 million trips in 2025.

title: Angela Rayner tells how Treasury to be stripped of powers in blow to London jobs
author: Nicholas Cecil
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Burnham To Give Mayors Share Of Income Tax.](https://cdn.ex.co/transformations-account/production/761715bb-261d-4032-af09-a493a82bd926/05fdaf12-51e2-55f3-96b1-9762b64dfd43/thumbnail-360.webp)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
It would retain the responsibility for overseeing the public finances.
![An aerial view of Parliament Square and government buildings including the Treasury in Whitehall (Victoria Jones/PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2025/03/21/10/abd716ffc00d27d25d8d3e4753a8f8efY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzQyNjM5MDk2-2.60844096.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Explaining the reforms, Ms Rayner told Times Radio: “It's about the whole of Government recognising that power that is centralised, which we're one of the most over-centralised economies, doesn't always give the best results for all areas.
“We've been keep trying to do that, and some people call it trickle down economics, and you've seen areas which were deindustrialised over the last sort of 50 years that haven't seen that investment and that drive come forward.”
She added: “So we now have an industrial strategy.
“We have a Government framework which is about putting power back in local people's hands, and then it's about delivery.
The devolution announcement came just days after ministers pressed ahead with plans for default planning approval for new homes within 800 metres or ten minutes walk of busy Tube, rail and tram stations.
The reform will be welcomed by many people desperate to find a home they can afford to rent or buy in London or other parts of the country.
But it sparked immediate protests that the policy runs counters to Mr Burnham’s pledge to devolve more powers, by stripping councils of key decision-making, and threatens to lead to more homes on green belt land.
Read More
Ms Rayner was speaking after the Prime Minister said the new No10 North will take responsibility for growth from the Treasury as part of his blueprint for the biggest “devolution of power in modern times”.
![Prime Minister Andy Burnham said ‘we will be there in Ukraine’s hour of need’ (Finnbarr Webster/PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/18/12/fdd383dcf39c0b7597a38f2e4546db93Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3MTM4MDE0-2.85564288.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Mr Burnham suggested the Treasury would focus on controlling the public finances while his outpost of 10 Downing Street based in Manchester would lead the charge on boosting the economy.
In an interview with The Times, he said Chancellor John Healey was fully supportive of the move which he described as part of a “huge transfer of power”.
“There’s a job to be done around control of public finances. It’s just the dual job of growth and control of public finances (that) sometimes clouds the growth mission,” he said.
“And particularly having No 10 leading on that growth mission means you’ve got maximum power to unlock the blockages where they exist in the wider Whitehall system.”
The Manchester branch of Downing Street in Heron House is already up and running and officials claim it will cost taxpayers no extra money.
The Prime Minister is expected to work at the outpost once each week during his premiership, as part of his move to push power out of Westminster.
However, Mr Burnham risks accusations of a power grab with No10 North taking control of the economic growth agenda, rather than this being shifted to the Treasury’s campus in Darlington.
summary: Angela Rayner announced reforms that will shift economic growth responsibilities from the Treasury to a new Manchester-based No10 North outpost, as part of a major decentralization of government power. While the Treasury will retain control over public finances, the move aims to address over-centralization and better support deindustrialised areas. However, the policy has sparked debate over potential impacts on local decision-making and council powers.
key_points: Responsibility for economic growth is being shifted from the Treasury to the new No10 North based in Manchester.
The Treasury will retain its core responsibility for overseeing public finances.
Angela Rayner stated that the reforms aim to counter over-centralized economic policies that have failed to invest in deindustrialised areas.
The Prime Minister is expected to work from the Manchester outpost once a week as part of efforts to push power out of Westminster.

title: Ridge appoints new project and programme delivery leader for London
author: Rockwool
content:
Appointment part of move to grow the function in the capital
Ridge has appointed a new partner for project and programme delivery.
The firm said Giles Heather has been tasked to grow its team in London, handling programme leadership, project controls, project management and portfolio management for clients across the capital.
The appointment comes as the consultant moves to grow its capabilities in the programme delivery of complex projects. Last year it acquired project management specialist Adept Management.

Heather has more than 18 years experience in programme and project delivery across various sectors, with much of his career spent at Turner & Townsend and more recently Linesight.

summary: Ridge has appointed Giles Heather as a new partner to lead and expand its project and programme delivery team in London. Heather brings over 18 years of experience from previous roles at Turner & Townsend and Linesight. This appointment supports the firm's ongoing strategy to strengthen its capabilities in managing complex projects within the capital.
