Numerous live music gigs and festivals are scheduled, including Waterworks Extended and HowTheLightGetsIn London.

title: Windrush line disrupted after fire at South Bermondsey waste centre
author: Harry Low; James W Kelly; Yang Tian
content:
Video shows moments after the fire broke out
- Published
Some London Overground trains remain suspended after a fire involving 50 tonnes of household waste "severely damaged" a recycling facility in south-east London.
Fifteen fire engines were called to Landmann Way in South Bermondsey shortly before 20:00 BST on Tuesday, according to London Fire Brigade (LFB), which said the fire was brought under control six hours later.
No services are running on the Windrush line from Surrey Quays to New Cross and Clapham Junction "due to an unsafe structure next to the railway". Trains from Highbury and Islington to West Croydon are severely delayed.
The LFB said the cause of the fire was not yet known. Firefighters tackled a blaze at the same facility in June.
Speaking from the scene, station commander Duncan Rees said: "Crews worked hard in difficult conditions to bring the fire under control."
He added that ladders were used to tackle the flames from above.
![Smoke rises over buildings. River Thames is in foreground](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/d491/live/715ebd70-9b96-11f1-8663-5b9301c10e82.jpg)
London Fire Brigade received more than 160 reports of a fire
Crews from East Greenwich, Old Kent Road, Deptford and surrounding fire stations were dispatched to the scene.
Rail services into London Bridge from New Cross were affected due to the fire blocking railway lines, National Rail said.
"Trains between these stations may be cancelled, severely delayed by up to 100 minutes or revised," it said on Tuesday.
![A cyclist watches besides a blue railing as plumes of black smoke drift into the sky above the yellow recycling facility.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1440/cpsprodpb/94a9/live/8b443d10-9b9a-11f1-a4e6-dfdb59e74cb0.jpg)
The fire caused rail disruption between London Bridge and New Cross
Rachael Jardine, a freelance journalist based in New Cross, told BBC London that trains on a nearby overground track were continuing to pass despite the "thick black smoke".
A local resident said he had first spotted the blaze while cycling home.
"I was coming back from Tescos and I could see the smoke from the road," he said.
"We cycled back to mine and realised it was just across the road... it's pretty mental."
Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
summary: A fire involving 50 tonnes of household waste severely damaged a recycling facility in South Bermondsey, requiring 15 fire engines and six hours to bring under control. The incident has caused ongoing disruption and suspensions on the London Overground Windrush line due to an unsafe structure next to the railway. The cause of the fire is currently unknown, though the same facility experienced a blaze previously in June.
key_points: A fire broke out at a recycling facility on Landmann Way in South Bermondsey involving 50 tonnes of household waste.
London Overground services on the Windrush line remain suspended between Surrey Quays, New Cross, and Clapham Junction.
The suspension is due to an unsafe structure next to the railway resulting from the fire.
The London Fire Brigade brought the blaze under control after six hours, and the cause is not yet known.

title: Fire rips through house in north London with roof completely destroyed
author: Tom Place
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![How to stop wildfires destroying your home as Fire Brigade warns of ‘new normal’ for London](https://cdn.ex.co/transformations-account/production/761715bb-261d-4032-af09-a493a82bd926/768f0a77-48dc-4ae5-80a7-1feeb1b0ffd2/thumbnail-360.webp)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
London Fire Brigade confirmed that they first received reports of the fire at around 7.10pm.
![The fire completely destroyed the roof of the property in Stanmore on Monday](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/18/14/03/london-road-pic-1_cropped.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Crews from Stanmore, Mill Hill, Harrow, Hendon, Wembley fire stations, as well as firefighters from Hertfordshire Fire and Rescue, mobilised to the scene, with fire over by around 10pm.
An LFB spokesperson said: "This incident is a reminder of just how important it is to have working smoke alarms in your home. Smoke alarms give the earliest possible warning when a fire starts.
"We encourage everyone to have smoke alarms fitted in every room where a fire could start, plus a heat alarm in the kitchen. It's important to test them regularly."
summary: A fire severely damaged a house in Stanmore, north London, completely destroying its roof on Monday. The London Fire Brigade received reports of the blaze at approximately 7.10pm and had it under control by around 10pm. Crews from multiple local fire stations and Hertfordshire Fire and Rescue responded to the incident.
key_points: A house fire in Stanmore completely destroyed the property's roof.
The London Fire Brigade responded to reports of the fire around 7.10pm on Monday.
Fire crews from multiple London stations and Hertfordshire Fire and Rescue tackled the blaze.
The fire was brought under control by approximately 10pm.
The London Fire Brigade emphasized the importance of having working smoke alarms.

title: Meet the modern-day Medicis: inside the glamorous world of London's young patrons
author: Isolde Walters
content:
After dark in London’s haute cultural institutions, a new social scene is emerging. Insiders, on any given evening, will find a coterie of bright young things swirling martinis beneath the startled gaze of Whistlejacket in the National Gallery, or grazing on canapés after hours among the marble statues in the Cast Courts at the V&A Museum. Forget benefactors in twinsets and pearls, these modern-day Medicis are young and well-connected, with deep pockets and a penchant for parties, couture and access.
Welcome to the world of the young patrons: a fresh generation of philanthropists, armed with Amexes and ambition. They are, of course, being welcomed famously. The V&A, Tate, National Gallery, Serpentine and Wallace Collection have all created young patrons’ schemes. In return for an annual fee of around £1,200 and with the hope that one or two of these budding Peggy Guggenheims may in time become big-deal donors (the type with their name on the wing) there are prodigious perks. Think behind-the-scenes tours, invitations to glitzy opening nights, summer parties, studio visits, mystery dinners, rooftop drinks and lavish trips to Paris, Turin and private Venetian palazzos. For the young, cultured rich, it is the ultimate status symbol.
The Marchioness of Bute has announced she is closing her eponymous fashion label, Serena Bute London. The clothes – loved by Poppy Delevingne, Rita Ora and so many more – never looked more glamorous than when they were modelled by Serena and her daughter, Lady Lola, at the family seat of Mount Stuart, the staggering four-storey Victorian Gothic fantasy on the Hebridean Isle of Bute
![article image](https://media.tatler.com/photos/6141e125797f8a06f4b68170/master/w_775%2Cc_limit/tatler-bute-6.jpg)
The schemes fly under the radar with very little advertisement, so although they are technically open to anyone who will pony up the yearly fee, in practise they operate like private members’ clubs, with patrons coming via word-of-mouth and personal recommendation. And, like any hot scene, it’s becoming tribal.
You’ll find the financiers and lawyers populating the National Gallery’s Young Ambassadors programme, where there’s an air of seriousness and perhaps – according to one art-world insider – fustiness. The V&A’s set is rather more feminine, sequinned and, many say, fun, with the lure of a sought-after invitation to the museum’s summer party a key draw. The Tate clique is very south London, with a taste for social causes and conceptual fashion; while the World Monuments Fund crowd is unabashedly international. Meanwhile you’ll find fashionistas flocking to the Serpentine’s Future Contemporaries young patrons programme.
Heading to Oxford? Whether you're a religious rower, a union hack, or a Right Hon, as results day rolls around, here's a totally objective, comprehensive guide to the college you're about to call home
But there’s no competition when it comes to which scheme reigns supreme on the London social scene. ‘The number one has to be the V&A’ says Žanete Bukarte, a Latvian lawyer and hobby sculptor, who is a young patron of four different institutions, including the museum in South Kensington. ‘The V&A curated a very vibrant crowd, helped by the location of the museum and word-of-mouth.’ Euthymia Procopé, the social butterfly hired to scatter a little society dust over the V&A’s young patrons’ programme, is in full agreement. ‘It is the jewel in the crown,’ she declares.
Established in 2016, and inspired by similar schemes at MoMA and the Frick in New York, the V&A Young Patron’s Circle began with the long-term goal of engaging young people in the hope that they would become absolute devotees of the museum and ideally, budding philanthropists. With a wide age range of 20 to 40, the scheme attracted international students as well as established lawyers and hedgefunders. And with jewellery designer Cora Sheibani – daughter of Bruno Bischofberger, the prominent Swiss art dealer known for his close associations with Jean-Michel Basquiat and Andy Warhol – as a founding co-chair, the programme wielded social power from the outset.
But Procopé, the scheme’s senior manager from 2021 to 2023, knew she could turn it up a notch, and she set about making the Young Patrons’ Circle a hotbed of socialites, redesigning its brochures and bringing in Flora Vesterberg as her co-chair.
The great and the gilded flocked to South Somerset when billionaire Koos Bekker built The Newt hotel. Some locals, however, feared it brought an end to their countryside way of life. Isolde Walters investigated the feud igniting the Green and Pleasant Land.
![Image may contain: Grass, Nature, Outdoors, Park, Plant, Land, Vegetation, Tree, Woodland, Scenery, Water, and Architecture](https://media.tatler.com/photos/6a7b022d9a0d012454c1c599/master/w_775%2Cc_limit/The%2520Newt%2520Estate.%2520The%2520Newt%2520In%2520Somerset.%2520Credit%2520The%2520Newt%2520In%2520Somerset.jpg)
‘I wanted to make it really sociable, and Flora was great,’ she says. ‘She would invite Amelia Windsor and Princess Beatrice to the Young Patrons’ annual party.’ Freddie and Sophie Windsor attended two years on the trot, rubbing shoulders with Tatler’s social editor Davina Chelsea. Society’s favourite royal DJ, Cassius Taylor, took over the decks in front of the museum’s medieval and Renaissance sculptures in 2023, while this year the patrons decamped to the V&A’s new east London outpost, where Tristram Hunt held court with Lord Ogilvy.
The strategy worked, and during Procopé and Vesterberg’s tenure, Viscountess Newport, Petrina Hesketh, the Countess of Belfast and Pamela Weinstock-Perry all became Young Patrons. But to keep the It girls happy, the perks had to match the parties. ‘The USP was that you’d get this incredible access to the museum out of hours… first-thing-in-the-morning visits and curator-led tours,’ says Procopé. There were trips abroad to tighten those all-important social bonds – such as the 2022 trip to Florence, which took in the Donatello exhibition at Palazzo Strozzi and a tour of Gucci’s private design archives, before finishing up with a drinks party at the former home of John Pope-Hennessy, one of the previous directors of the museum.
Romance occasionally flourishes between young patrons. ‘People do use it as a dating opportunity,’ Procopé says. ‘I know of several examples where romance has absolutely struck. You’d notice on day trips – people talking a lot and holding hands.’
But for socialites in search of The One, the V&A’s unfavourable female-to-male ratio is hardly ideal. According to one insider, the only patron’s programme to join if on the hunt for love is the National Gallery’s Young Ambassadors, as it’s where the men, with reassuringly high-flying careers in law, finance and tech, are. Former Tatler cover star Sabine Getty teamed up with Harriet Roseberry as co-chairs to launch the £1,200-a-year membership in 2021. A year later, financier Jacques-Louis de la Beraudiere and art tech CEO Sam Glatman were among the eligibles on board.
Bukarte, who is also a Young Ambassador (the scheme’s name is a nod to the gallery’s famous Holbein painting), describes the hallowed institution’s youthful coterie as a ‘very elegant, very poised crowd, full of people who are deeply knowledgeable about the art world already, or hold very important roles in the finance or legal worlds. Very adult, quite serious.’ That comes with its challenges. One Young Ambassador, who shall remain nameless, describes the group as ‘academic’, with room for improvement when it comes to parties. ‘It’s such a huge space to fill – you have to have so many people there for it to feel like a vibe… There was a party for the Sainsbury Wing, and there were hundreds and hundreds of people there; it didn’t really feel as friendly and intimate as the V&A parties.’
The Junior Board of the World Monuments Fund has no such difficulty with its parties – the last one was a lavish affair at Horace Walpole’s neo-Gothic Strawberry Hill mansion. Data scientist Ege Gürmeriçliler, who serves as a co-chair, was the star attraction. ‘He’s gorgeous and extraordinarily rich, and the girls were all over him like bees on honey,’ one attendee recalls. ‘He spends all day working on AI models in his flat in west London, but he pours his passion into the World Monuments Fund.’
Buried in the Surrey Hills, Beaverbrook once played host to an earlier generation of Hollywood greats. This week, it was the turn of tinseltown’s reigning king and queen: Tom Holland and Zendaya, who celebrated their marriage by booking out the entire estate. But there’s so much beyond the caviar-infused omakase and chequerboard swimming pool, reveals Delilah Khomo
![article image](https://media.tatler.com/photos/618910e137fe9b2985bd366f/master/w_775%2Cc_limit/Beaverbrookspa0892%2520%2520.jpeg)
The contrast between a serious (and often lucrative) career and the opportunity to lose oneself in art in the evenings is key for young patrons. ‘The finance tribe love the contrast between crunching numbers and then coming to something arty as a change of scene,’ says Procopé. There is also the ageless flex of art patronage – just as the Medicis realised the cultural capital to be gained from supporting Michelangelo and da Vinci, today’s young patrons are using the prestige in a uniquely 21st-century manner. ‘People put it in their LinkedIn profiles and on their Instagram bios,’ Procopé says. ‘People like the cachet of being able to say, “I am a patron, I am a supporter of this art institution” – and it does carry social clout.’
Then there’s the access. For a relatively affordable annual membership fee, society’s doors are thrown open to the young patron. You may find yourself at a World Monuments Fund event, mixing with the youngest generation of the Niarchos family or travelling with the heiress to the Bacardi fortune. ‘It’s a brilliant way of meeting people,’ Bukarte enthuses. ‘You get exposed to people a regular person would not. Most of these people are not that regular: they are very well-connected, or come from prominent families.’
Unsurprisingly, the Tate's Young Patrons are more democratic – they get a say on how funds they raise are spent by the museum – and they are more interested in social causes. While the young art aficionados have flown on Tate trips before, now a sustainability drive means only destinations accessible by Eurostar are on the cards. Still, they managed to net Princess Eugenie as an ambassador and arranged parties in the Tank Rooms at Tate Modern, rooftop soirées, and back-to-school drinks at the Arts Club, Ladbroke Hall and Annabel’s.
Gulru Arvas, an architect based in west London but originally from Istanbul, who served as a co-chair, describes the tribe as a diverse mix of professions. ‘At a young patrons’ dinner, I would chat with an artist, then someone who works in finance, a mathematician, someone in film and another patron in oil and gas.’ The dress code? ‘edgy, a lot of Margiela, that kind of thing.’
Arvas – known as Gu – has just become a member of the Serpentine Galleries’ young patrons’ scheme, Future Contemporaries, lured by the VIP breakfast at Zaha Hadid-designed restaurant The Magazine –‘it’s a really fun way to kick of Frieze Week’ – and the gallery’s Mystery Nights, where young patrons are split up into small groups, and given a time and a place to meet and dine in the fabulous homes of select art collectors. The difference between the Tate crowd and the Serpentine crowd? ‘They dress up a little more.’ Think all-black and very fashion.
Many young patrons can’t resist supporting multiple institutions, which can make their social calendar even more hectic, particularly during summer party week or when Frieze is on.‘There is a tribe that belongs to all of these groups and circulates around, going to several events per evening, running from the Tate to the Serpentine,’ Bukarte says. ‘That forms a community element in its own right, because if you attend these gatherings for a sufficient period of time, you already know who the other people are who go to these institutions as well. Often you share a black cab and run around London with these people. You end up going to dinner together or going to 5 Hertford Street afterwards, as many of these events take place on a Thursday night.’
With rumours that the British Museum and National Portrait Gallery are soon to launch their own young patrons’ programmes, and with the Wallace Collection’s Young Benefactors scheme attracting new members, the hot young philanthropists striding through the capital’s cultural scene are set to multiply.
The only question left to ask is: what tribe of young patrons do you belong to? The art might be priceless, but the guest list is the real masterpiece.
This feature was originally published in the January 2026 issue of Tatler and remains unedited.
![](https://media.tatler.com/photos/6a621fc310c1821925786e55/1:1/w_200%2Cc_limit/RGB-09-26Cover4ColNoPrice.jpg)
summary: London's major cultural institutions, including the V&A, Tate, and National Gallery, have established young patrons' schemes targeting affluent individuals aged 20 to 40. For an annual fee of around £1,200, members gain access to exclusive perks such as after-hours tours, international trips, and high-profile social events. These programs function similarly to private members' clubs, offering participants a mix of networking, romance, and cultural prestige.
key_points: Institutions like the V&A, Tate, National Gallery, Serpentine, and World Monuments Fund offer young patron memberships for roughly £1,200 a year.
Perks include private curator-led tours, exclusive parties, and international trips to locations like Florence and Venice.
Different museums attract distinct social tribes, ranging from the V&A's glamorous society crowd to the National Gallery's finance-heavy Young Ambassadors.
Membership provides high-status networking opportunities, social clout, and access to well-connected peers and prominent families.

title: Man found shot dead inside vehicle in Newham
author: James W Kelly
content:
![A white Toyota Prius with visible front-end damage parked on a residential London street lined with cars, situated in front of a white and blue Metropolitan Police Service (MPS) forensic tent. A blue circular "One way" arrow sign and a street number ("412") are visible on the building behind the tent.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/9f9e/live/54877de0-9b0a-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Officers were called to St Bartholomew's Road, Newham, at about 03:00 BST
- Published
A man in his 40s has been found shot dead inside a car in east London, the Metropolitan Police said.
A murder investigation has begun after officers were called to St Bartholomew's Road, Newham, at about 03:00 BST and found a man with gunshot wounds, the force said.
He was pronounced dead at the scene. The man's family have been informed and are being supported by specialist officers.
A police cordon remains in place on St Bartholomew's Road and no arrests have yet been made.
At the scene, a police evidence tent could be seen behind a white Toyota Prius, which had collided with a black Range Rover.
Abdul Qadir, owner of the Range Rover, said: "My daughter heard the car alarm go off and she heard the shots, like a bomb. She heard the impact of two vehicles. And I heard people running off.
"It's the third time my car's been collided with â so I thought it's 03:00, I'm not going out to investigate.
"I just went back to sleep, because I know this happens around here.
"Then up to 10 minutes after I heard people gathering. They said someone had been shot."
'It's upsetting'
A man who lives nearby, who did not want to be named, said: "Around 03:00 or 04:00 I heard a crash and then a car alarm going on, and then it went off."
He said he looked outside about an hour later, but did not see anything.
A woman who lives a short distance from the police cordon said: "We heard a bullet noise first and then a car driving very quickly.
"We thought it was boys racing. We came to know in the morning someone had been shot."
A woman, who did not want to be named, said she woke up to find the police cordon outside her house.
She said she had lived in the area for more than 50 years and usually felt safe.
She said crime was increasing in the area, but added: "It's the same everywhere isn't it?"
Another resident said: "It's made me feel really uneasy, I was going to go to work this morning and didn't because I didn't want to leave the kids.
"It's upsetting, I think this is the first time something like this has happened nearby. Generally we feel pretty safe, now we might not feel as safe."
Det Ch Insp Dan Whitten said: "We know this incident will cause concern in the local area, and I want to reassure the community that my team and I are doing everything we can to determine what happened and trace those responsible.
"Those in the area will continue to see an increased police presence throughout the day while these inquiries continue."
He asked for anyone with information on the death to come forward to police.
According to UK government data, there were 32 homicides by shooting in England and Wales between April 2024 and March 2025, accounting for 6% of all homicides.

summary: A man in his 40s was found shot dead inside a vehicle on St Bartholomew's Road in Newham at around 03:00 BST. The Metropolitan Police have launched a murder investigation, and the victim's family has been informed. No arrests have been made as police maintain a cordon and appeal for information from the public.
key_points: A murder investigation has been launched by the Metropolitan Police following the fatal shooting of a man in his 40s.
Officers responded to St Bartholomew's Road in Newham at about 03:00 BST and found the victim inside a car with gunshot wounds.
The man was pronounced dead at the scene, and his family is being supported by specialist officers.
No arrests have been made yet, and police have established a cordon with an increased presence in the area.
Local residents reported hearing gunshots, a crash involving the victim's car and a Range Rover, and people running away.

title: TfL urged to prioritise investment in escalators
author: Kumail Jaffer
content:
![General view of a triple escalator at Liverpool Street station. Two are going up and one is going down. Various passengers are standing on all escalators.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/a9e1/live/7a77b300-98ba-11f1-9a0b-ef36d15fc6b3.jpg)
Transport for London must make escalators a funding priority, a Labour London Assembly member has said
- Published
Transport for London (TfL) must spend more to refurbish and replace ageing escalators on the London Underground, a senior London Assembly member has said.
Elly Baker, the transport spokesperson for the City Hall Labour group, said this infrastructure needed to be prioritised to ensure the mayor's active transport targets were feasible.
Freedom of Information data released in July revealed 153 out of 566 escalators â over a quarter â on the Underground were operating beyond their expected shelf life.
TfL has said it works "hard to keep our escalators in good working order, and this includes regular safety checks and a proactive rolling maintenance programme".
![Close-up of Baker who is looking past the camera with a neutral expression. She has short brown hair and hoop earrings.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/470/cpsprodpb/c4f1/live/e7fc5d00-98be-11f1-9a0b-ef36d15fc6b3.png)
Elly Baker, the transport spokesperson for the City Hall Labour group, says escalators must be a top priority
In 2025-26, TfL spent Â£56.1m on escalators, including Â£38.6m of operating expenditure and Â£17.5m of capital expenditure to upgrade, renew and modernise the assets, according to the mayor's office.
In the same period, TfL spent Â£1.3m on "reactive maintenance call-outs for escalators".
Baker said: "It's really important that we make sure escalators are working on the Tube â [but] I am concerned that TfL aren't giving it enough of a priority."
City Hall has a target for 80% of journeys in London to be made by foot, bicycle or public transport by 2041.
Baker said TfL had recently shifted from a model where they would refurbish escalators after 20 years and completely replace them after 40 years to taking a "risk-based approach", where escalators are closely monitored, to save money.
This had led to "more and more escalators going out of service unexpectedly", which in turn, risked putting people off using the network altogether, she argued.
![Broken escalator with missing steps](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/c40d/live/df8604f0-98b9-11f1-9a0b-ef36d15fc6b3.jpg)
Last year three out of four escalators at Woolwich Arsenal DLR Station were out of action, including one at the Greens End entrance, which is still broken
A TfL spokesperson said 95% of escalators were available to passengers, "despite heavy usage", adding: "Inevitably, a small number of escalators have had to be temporarily withdrawn from service or are subject to increased maintenance and inspection regimes to ensure they can continue operating with acceptable levels of reliability.
"Funding for replacing these highly complex machines is subject to a prioritisation process which examines assets across the whole TfL network, looking at customer usage and the latest safety and condition assessments."
Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
summary: Transport for London (TfL) must prioritize funding for the refurbishment and replacement of ageing escalators on the London Underground, according to City Hall Labour transport spokesperson Elly Baker. Freedom of Information data shows that over a quarter of the network's escalators are operating beyond their expected shelf life, which Baker argues risks deterring passengers. While TfL maintains that 95% of its escalators are available and subject to regular maintenance, a shift from scheduled replacements to a risk-based approach has led to concerns over unexpected outages.
key_points: Over a quarter of London Underground escalators (153 out of 566) are operating beyond their expected shelf life.
Elly Baker argues that failing to prioritize escalator investment risks undermining active transport targets and putting people off using the network.
TfL has shifted from a fixed-schedule refurbishment and replacement model to a risk-based monitoring approach to save money.
TfL stated that 95% of its escalators remain available for passengers despite heavy usage and a prioritization process for funding across the network.

title: Why is feeding deer in The Royal Parks a problem?
author: Jess Warren
content:
![A sign at Richmond Park telling visitors not to feed the deer.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/3505/live/268038a0-9aed-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
- Published
Visitors to London's Royal Parks are being reminded that it is illegal , externalto feed the wild deer after a man was injured by a stag that approached his picnic group.
From safety risks to photographing deer responsibly, here is what you need to know about the deer in Richmond Park and Bushy Park.
Why are people being told not to feed the deer?
Visitors to south-west London's Richmond and Bushy parks are being urged not to feed the red and fallow deer or get within 50m (165ft) of the animals.
On Saturday, a man in his 60s suffered chest injuries after being attacked by a stag in Richmond Park when it approached his picnic group.
The deer was subsequently shot by a Royal Parks wildlife officer as it was deemed a danger to visitors.
![A black and white image taken in September 1936 of a visitor to Richmond Park reading a Royal Parks notice warning people about "Danger from Deer".](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/9684/live/e42dcba0-9ae9-11f1-930b-57cfba7235f9.jpg)
Visitors to Richmond and Bushy parks have been told for decades not to feed the deer
Paul Richards, park manager at Richmond Park, said the animal's behaviour was likely the direct result of having previously been fed by visitors at the park.
"It is only because people had fed this particular animal that its behaviour had changed," he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
The "do not feed" warning is not new. The Royal Parks has regularly told people visiting both of the south-west London parks not to feed the wild animals.
How can feeding deer put people at risk?
The deer in both parks are wild animals, and can act unpredictably around humans.
Unlike deer in other places, such as the city of Nara in Japan where deer are regularly fed by people, London's deer should not be approached or fed.
Richards said the deer in The Royal Parks had begun to associate visitors with food, which was "not their natural behaviour".
"Enjoy the deer, respect the deer, keep a safe distance from the deer," he said.
"Don't feed them, they don't need feeding. Some people think they're doing a good deed. In fact you're not, you're doing quite the opposite."
Richards said that if fed, the deer began to associate people with food and would be more likely to approach groups or individuals in the park.
This, he warned, was dangerous to visitors and put them at risk of serious injury.
Feeding deer may also increase the risk of them ingesting plastic, which blocks their stomachs and causes malnutrition.
My children want to pet the deer, why is that not allowed?
Last month, families with young children were seen trying to stroke the deer in Richmond Park.
Richards said his team were "shocked and extremely concerned" by video footage from the park, and called the actions "deeply irresponsible and highly dangerous".
The park manager explained that closing in on the animals would cause the deer stress and risked a "fatal incident".
"Richmond Park's red and fallow deer are wild, powerful animals. Although they may appear calm, they can react suddenly and aggressively if they feel threatened," he said.
"Stags can weigh more than 25 stone (159kg) and run at speeds of up to 30mph (48km/h), making them highly dangerous if visitors get too close."
Do the deer have enough food in the drought?
Red and fallow deer eat grasses, leaves and shoots of trees, as well as acorns, sweet chestnuts and horse chestnuts.
Richards said: "They don't need to be fed. A lot of people are thinking: 'It's bone dry out there, everything is brown', but the deer don't need supplementary feeding here at Richmond Park."
![A deer reaching up to eat leaves from a tree in Richmond Park.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/b83e/live/d7565f30-9aeb-11f1-930b-57cfba7235f9.jpg)
Deer eat grasses, leaves, acorns, sweet chestnuts and horse chestnuts
"There's plenty of things for them to eat," he added. "They're grazing on bramble, we're already seeing a bit of an early autumn, and it won't be long before sweet chestnuts are beginning to fall, so there is plenty of food for them."
Visitors are urged not to remove conkers (horse chestnuts) from the park as they are a vital part of the deer's diet and help to build up their fat reserves for winter.
How can I photograph the deer?
London's deer population is much-loved and photographed, due to their apparent juxtaposition with city-life.
The current 630-strong herd of wild red and fallow deer in Richmond Park were first introduced by Charles I in 1637 and roam freely amongst the trees and grasslands.
They have been enjoyed by visitors for decades, but must be respected, Richards said.
![A woman stands beneath a tree to photograph stags in Richmond Park.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/869/cpsprodpb/775b/live/64f843e0-9aeb-11f1-930b-57cfba7235f9.jpg)
Visitors are told to photograph deer through a zoom lens
"The deer here are wild, they have been here for centuries," he said.
"If you want to photograph them, photograph them using the zoom function on your phone or camera."
He said visitors must keep a distance of 50m (165ft) from the animals.
What should you do if a deer approaches you in a Royal Park?
Visitors are told to never feed or touch the deer in Richmond and Bushy parks.
If one comes towards you, put all food and packaging out of sight and move away slowly and calmly, The Royal Parks says.
People should not try to move the deer away themselves.
"If you witness someone putting themselves, others or the deer at risk, please do not try and intervene but report it immediately to the police," a Royal Parks spokesperson says.
Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
summary: Visitors to London's Richmond and Bushy parks are legally prohibited from feeding the wild deer because it alters their behavior and creates safety risks. A recent incident involving a man injured by a stag led to the animal being shot, highlighting the dangers of approaching or feeding the park's wildlife. Park officials stress that the deer have sufficient natural food sources and urge the public to maintain a distance of at least 50 meters.
key_points: Feeding the wild deer in Richmond and Bushy parks is illegal.
A man in his 60s suffered chest injuries after being attacked by a stag that approached his picnic group, leading to the animal being shot.
Feeding causes deer to associate humans with food, leading them to approach visitors and increasing the risk of plastic ingestion.
Visitors are advised to keep a distance of 50 meters, avoid petting or feeding the animals, and use zoom lenses for photography.

title: Rain finally falls in London! Capital rejoices as showers hit city with more to come
author: Matt Watts; Tom Place
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![UK: DRONE - London parks dry out amid prolonged heat and lack of rain.](https://cdn.ex.co/transformations-account/production/761715bb-261d-4032-af09-a493a82bd926/e635ba55-b89a-5b3d-ac13-c3a16b31b9f4/thumbnail-360.webp)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
Londoners woke on Tuesday to puddles on the streets, while others celebrated as they heard the rain in the early hours.
The tracker showed rain hitting most of the city - some parts of which haven’t seen any real rain for almost two months.
![Puddles could be seen on streets and pavements in the capital on Tuesday morning](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/18/5/20/rain-London.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
It comes after England saw the driest July on record - with no meaningful rain in London.
Across the Thames catchment area, just 0.8mm of rain was recorded - a mere 2% of the long-term average.
Many Londoners took to social media to celebrate after the rain fell overnight.
Multiple forecasters are also predicting more rain to fall in the capital in the coming days, with further showers expected later on Tuesday.
Light rain showers are also forecast for Wednesday, Thursday and Friday by BBC weather, and the Met Office is also predicting a chance of showers on those days.
Read More
Most of the showers will fall across parts of north-west England, Northern Ireland and southern Scotland, with some parts of south-east England staying dry.
summary: Rain finally fell in London on Tuesday morning after nearly two months without real rain, following England's driest July on record. Residents celebrated the showers on social media as puddles formed across the city streets. Forecasters predict further rain and light showers for the capital in the coming days.
key_points: London received its first significant rain in nearly two months on Tuesday morning.
England experienced its driest July on record, with London seeing no meaningful rainfall.
Residents celebrated the arrival of the rain on social media.
Forecasters including the Met Office and BBC Weather predict more showers for the capital through the rest of the week.

title: Muslim woman threatened on London bus says abuse is daily
author: Alice Bhandhukravi; Jess Warren
content:
![Salsabil in a blue niqab and headscarf, standing in front of a blue wall.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/924/cpsprodpb/91a3/live/3cce26b0-9afe-11f1-a27d-25dca26018ed.png)
Salsabil says she is regularly abused because of her religious clothing
- Published
A Muslim woman who was abused on a bus in west London for wearing a niqab has said that she is subjected to Islamophobic abuse on a daily basis in the capital.
"Spitting, barging, pushing. It happens to me every single day," says 21-year-old Salsabil.
"We kind of convince ourselves that this is something we have to tolerate rather than report."
A spokesperson for the Metropolitan Police said that "no community in London should have to endure intimidation or abuse" and the force was "committed to tackling all forms of hate crime".
Salsabil said she was travelling home from central London on 31 July when she was verbally abused because of her niqab, a veil for her face that leaves the area around the eyes clear and is worn with a headscarf.
She got off the bus and said she boarded the next one, and was again subjected to verbal abuse regarding her niqab. The incident was captured on video.
"He was swearing at me for the way I'm dressed," Salsabil said.
"I went to go sit down and this passenger stopped me, again, very aggressively, telling me that I'm not welcome with this veil on my face, that this is terrorism, this is not religion.
"He said that if I refuse to take off my veil that he will take it off for me."
Salsabil said the man threatened to kill her, and another passenger intervened and became embroiled in a punch-up with the man.
She said he was the only passenger who came to her defence.
The bus driver intervened and the man was asked to get off, which he did, and Salsabil got off at her normal stop in north-west London.
"I genuinely thought that I was going to be seriously injured," she said. "I felt so alone.
"I'm so grateful for the passenger who did step in and defend me."
'I haven't felt safe in the past year'
She added: "This happens to me really often. If I reported every single incident, I think I would probably just live at the police station."
Salsabil explained that she chose not to report the incident to the Metropolitan Police, after she previously reported an Islamophobic hate crime and officers "were quite dismissive about it".
She said: "A lot of women do report incidents like this and they are dismissed, and being dismissed is very demotivating to ever approach the police again.
"I was born and raised in London and I've always felt safe... but I think recently, for the past year, I haven't felt safe, especially going out on public transport," Salsabil added.
"We should never justify abuse based on how someone dresses," she said. "If a woman chooses to wear the hijab or the niqab, or doesn't choose to wear any religious clothing, she should never feel unsafe."
![A woman holds a smartphone while sitting on a park bench](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/fb42/live/c96d6cd0-9639-11f1-870d-5d08c49babb2.jpg)
The incident on the bus was captured on video and has been seen by the BBC
Siwan Hayward, Transport for London's (TfL) director of security, policing and enforcement, said she was "appalled" by the video of Salsabil being abused on the bus.
"No-one should ever have to fear or experience abuse when using our network," she said.
"We are urgently looking into this incident and encourage anyone who experienced or witnessed this incident to contact the police."
A spokesperson for the Met Police said they were aware of the video and were making efforts to contact the victim, and urged witnesses to report the incident to force.
Both TfL and the Met said they took a zero-tolerance approach to anti-Muslim hatred.
Data collected by the Met Police , externalshowed that reported faith hate crime rose by 25% in London over the past year, and there was a 31% rise in reported Islamophobic offences.
London's victims commissioner, Andrea Simon, said she did not believe Salsabil's experience was a "one-off".
"We have to be very concerned that this is something that's affecting particularly those who might be visibly identifiable by clothing as being Muslim or being of a faith background," she said.
"It's really concerning to hear that someone who was subjected to this kind of behaviour felt that they weren't able to report what had happened to them to the police, because they lacked confidence that anything would be done about it."
